title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
provider: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (administered by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration through Vibrant Emotional Health)
notes: Checked only to verify the contact methods named in the lesson's closing safety note: the Lifeline site states that a person can call, text, or chat with a counsellor at any hour. Used for the signpost alone; the lesson gives no crisis guidance and no self-management instruction.

title: About the ABCD Study
provider: Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study consortium, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health
notes: Official consortium page for the NIH-funded ABCD Study. Used for the study's description as the largest long-term study of brain development and child health in the United States, for its enrollment of 11,880 children aged 9 to 10 across 21 research sites, for its plan to follow them through adolescence into young adulthood, and for the breadth of what it tracks (brain imaging alongside sleep, screen use, sports, family, academic, and health measures). Cited in the lesson as evidence of how the field now studies developmental change, not as the source of any specific finding about a single child. Reuse terms are not stated for page text, so it is recorded reference only.

title: 2014 ACA Code of Ethics
provider: American Counseling Association
notes: Source for counseling's five core professional values and six fundamental principles (autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence, justice, fidelity, veracity), the Code's six purposes and nine sections, A.2 informed consent including types of information, developmental and cultural sensitivity, inability to give consent, and mandated clients, A.4.b personal values, I.1.b ethical decision making, and I.1.c conflicts between ethics and laws. Copyrighted; paraphrased only.

title: Comprehensive Family Assessment Guidelines for Child Welfare
provider: Children's Bureau, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (2005)
notes: Federal practice guidance. PDF text extracted and searched: the guidelines direct caseworkers to use the ecomap and genogram with parents to record family history and the current extended family and support system, and to add to both after meeting children and reviewing records, providers and the extended support system. Used to show these are working instruments in federally guided practice, not classroom exercises.

title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
provider: Office of Community Services, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
license: U.S. government work
notes: Program page read in full. Used to support the single claim that referral infrastructure is not limited to 211: the program directs people to the National Energy Assistance Referral line and to a locator site for information on how and where to apply locally, and states that the program does not provide direct grants to individuals. No eligibility criteria or benefit amounts are taken from this page.

title: About TANF
provider: Office of Family Assistance, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
notes: Page read in full; it states it is current as of 27 September 2024. Supports that TANF replaced Aid to Families with Dependent Children in 1996, that it is a block grant providing $16.6 billion annually to states, territories, the District of Columbia and federally recognized tribes, the four statutory purposes, and that jurisdictions have considerable flexibility subject to work participation and cost-sharing requirements. Also supports that the administering office publishes separate collections for laws and regulations, policy guidance, and reporting instructions - the basis for the sub-regulatory guidance point. No license is stated on the page; wording was not reproduced and the dollar figure is dated in the lesson.

title: Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program
provider: Administration for Community Living, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
notes: Program page read for the statutory basis in Title VII of the Older Americans Act (sections 711/712), the 2024 update to the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Programs rule at 45 CFR 1324, the core functions (identify, investigate and resolve complaints made by or on behalf of residents; provide information; ensure resident access; represent resident interests before government agencies; recommend changes in law), and the statement that the program operates in all states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and Guam with a full-time State Ombudsman directing each program.

title: Fact Sheet: New Rule on the Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps Provided by State and Local Governments
provider: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division (ADA.gov)
notes: Used for the 2024 Title II rule requiring state and local government entities - explicitly including public schools, community colleges, and public universities - to make web content and mobile apps conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, and for the compliance dates of April 26, 2027 (populations of 50,000 or more) and April 26, 2028 (smaller entities and special district governments). Used to establish that digital accessibility in U.S. public education is a legal floor rather than a courtesy. No wording reproduced; no legal advice given.

title: Guidelines for Writing About People With Disabilities
provider: ADA National Network / ADA Knowledge Translation Center (funded by the National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research)
notes: Fact sheet read for the contrast between person-first constructions (person with a disability, person who uses a wheelchair) and identity-first constructions (deaf person, autistic person), for the instruction to ask in order to find out an individual's language preference, and for the list of constructions to avoid (wheelchair-bound, handicapped, suffers from / victim framing, condescending terms such as special or differently-abled, and inspirational stereotyping). The fact sheet states it may be reproduced and distributed freely with attribution to the ADA National Network; even so, no wording is reproduced here.

title: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014 edition)
provider: Joint Committee on the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing of the American Educational Research Association, the American Psychological Association, and the National Council on Measurement in Education; published by AERA
notes: The full 2014 English edition PDF was read from the open-access files page maintained by the three sponsoring organizations. Used for the definition of validity as the degree to which evidence and theory support interpretations of test scores for proposed uses; for the explicit statement that it is the interpretation and not the test that is evaluated and that the unqualified phrase 'the validity of the test' is incorrect (Standard 1.0, Standard 1.1); for validity as a unitary concept and the deliberate replacement of historical validity types with five sources of validity evidence (test content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables, consequences of testing); for construct underrepresentation and construct-irrelevant variance; for the traceability criterion governing when consequences count as validity evidence; for chapter 2 on reliability/precision, replications, true score, classical test theory, generalizability theory, IRT information functions, the three families of reliability coefficients plus scorer consistency, KR-20 as the dichotomous special case of coefficient alpha, factors affecting reliability (test length, rater training, population variability), the standard error of measurement and conditional standard errors, Standard 2.0 on precision proportionate to stakes, Standard 2.6 on coefficients not being interchangeable, and the statement that blanket claims that a test 'is reliable' are rarely acceptable; and for chapter 3 on fairness, Standard 3.0, universal design, differential item functioning as a flag requiring substantive explanation, and the accommodation versus modification distinction. Copyright page states all rights reserved, so the text is free to read but nothing was reproduced or adapted.

title: Cultural Responsiveness in Education: Research Summary (plain language summary, June 2024)
provider: Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO), jointly funded by Australian Commonwealth, state and territory governments; retrieved as ERIC full text ED673953
license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the document, ISBN 978-1-923066-34-2 online)
notes: Full five-page summary extracted and read. Used for the finding that cultural responsiveness is a relatively nascent research field with limited causal evidence regarding effects on student outcomes; for the four stated reasons (variety of definitions, inconsistent operationalization, no standardized measures of culturally responsive practice, and disagreement about the outcomes it should affect); for the judgement that under AERO's standards of evidence it is not yet possible to identify specific practices that can confidently be considered evidence-based; and for the reported convergence in the literature on reciprocity, respect, relationships of trust and care, and teacher reflexivity. The document is Australian and framed around First Nations education, which the lesson does not misrepresent as a U.S. finding: it is cited as a second national research agency reaching a parallel conclusion. Licence is CC BY 4.0, so reuse would be permitted, but no passage was reproduced.

title: Community-based Participatory Research: Assessing the Evidence (Evidence Report/Technology Assessment No. 99)
provider: Viswanathan M, Ammerman A, Eng E, et al.; Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (US), Report No. 04-E022-2
license: Public domain (U.S. government work)
notes: Structured abstract and front matter read on NCBI Bookshelf. Supports the AHRQ definition of CBPR, the review scale (185 articles; 60 CBPR studies; 30 intervention studies of which 12 completed and evaluated), the finding that steering committees and advisory boards were the main decision-sharing mechanism but generally did not develop research questions or proposals, and the conclusion that strong community-institution collaboration was often not combined with solid research methods. NCBI marks this 2004 report as provided for historical reference; the lesson dates it accordingly.

title: Trauma Informed Care: A Systematic Review (AHRQ Publication No. 25-EHC007)
provider: Minnesota Evidence-based Practice Center for the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services; read on NCBI Bookshelf
license: Bookshelf record states the publication is in the public domain; AHRQ's own notice on the same page states that specific written permission is needed for commercial use or use outside the United States
notes: Structured abstract and front matter read. The single most important source for the lesson's evidence claim: searches through 19 July 2024, 4,379 unique references screened, 12 eligible studies in 16 publications across adult medical care, adult mental health, primary prevention for children, adolescent medical care and residential and non-residential child welfare; all studies high risk of bias; evidence insufficient for every outcome and comparison; no harms data collected; models vary considerably in components. The review's own caution - that insufficient evidence does not mean the interventions are useless - is reported in the lesson. Because the page carries two different statements about reuse, the record is conservative: findings reported, no wording reproduced.

title: Inner Speech: Development, Cognitive Functions, Phenomenology, and Neurobiology (Psychological Bulletin, 141(5), 931-965)
provider: Alderson-Day, B., & Fernyhough, C.; PubMed Central (PMC4538954)
license: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution License, as recorded for the article in Europe PMC)
notes: Open-access review (DOI 10.1037/bul0000021) used for inner speech as covert, self-directed verbal thinking implicated in accounts of cognitive development, executive function, and speech monitoring; for its developmental origin in overt self-directed (private) speech that becomes progressively internalized; and for the review's own caution that inner speech varies substantially between individuals and across the life span. Used to support the lesson's treatment of private speech as a developmental route from social dialogue to internal self-regulation, not as evidence that private speech straightforwardly predicts task performance.

title: Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? (Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1-18)
provider: Louis Alfieri, Patricia J. Brooks, Naomi J. Aldrich, Harriet R. Tenenbaum; ERIC record EJ933606
notes: Abstract retrieved through the ERIC API; bibliographic details confirmed (DOI 10.1037/a0021017). Used for the two meta-analyses across 164 studies: 580 comparisons favouring explicit instruction over unassisted discovery (d = -0.38, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.31]) and 360 comparisons favouring enhanced or assisted discovery over other forms of instruction (d = 0.30, 95% CI [0.23, 0.36]), and for the authors' conclusion that unassisted discovery does not benefit learners whereas feedback, worked examples, scaffolding and elicited explanations do. This is the lesson's empirical resolution of the inquiry question. Abstract-level verification; no wording reproduced.

title: The Effectiveness of Universal Design for Learning: A Systematic Review of the Literature and Meta-Analysis (Cogent Education, 10(1), 2218191)
provider: Qais I. Almeqdad, Abdullah M. Alodat, Mahmoud F. Alquraan, Mohammad A. Mohaidat, Ahmad K. Al-Makhzoomy; Education Resources Information Center (ERIC EJ1393594), IES, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Record and published abstract read via the ERIC record and the DOAJ article record (DOI 10.1080/2331186X.2023.2218191). Used for the inclusion of 13 empirical peer-reviewed pre-post studies published 2015-2021 across six countries, the observation that the studies mainly used a one-group quantitative research design, and the reported total effect size of 3.56 with considerable heterogeneity evident. Used in the lesson to illustrate that the UDL literature is small and methodologically uneven, not to assert an effect size for practice. Journal licence not confirmed on the retrieved record, so reference only.

title: Effects of the Expanded Child Tax Credit on Employment Outcomes: Evidence from Real-World Data from April to December 2021 (NBER Working Paper 29823)
provider: Elizabeth Ananat, Benjamin Glasner, Christal Hamilton and Zachary Parolin, National Bureau of Economic Research
notes: Working paper abstract read on the NBER site; not peer reviewed, and the lesson says so. Cited as the other documented side of the same disagreement: using Current Population Survey and Census Household Pulse data covering the six months of monthly payments in 2021, the authors report very small, inconsistently signed and statistically insignificant effects on employment and labour force participation among adults in households with children. Paired with the Corinth et al. paper to show students a genuine methodological dispute (ex ante simulation of a permanent policy against ex post estimation of a temporary one) rather than a resolved answer.

title: The enduring effects of abuse and related adverse experiences in childhood: a convergence of evidence from neurobiology and epidemiology (European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 256(3), 174-186)
provider: Anda RF, Felitti VJ, Bremner JD, Walker JD, Whitfield C, Perry BD, Dube SR, Giles WH; Springer, author manuscript on PubMed Central
notes: Read on PubMed Central for the study-population facts the 1998 abstract does not carry: the ACE Study is a collaboration between Kaiser Permanente's Health Appraisal Center in San Diego and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; the full sample was 17,337 adult HMO members (9,367 women, 7,970 men; mean age 56 and 58); 73 percent of women and 76 percent of men were white; 34 percent of women and 45 percent of men were college graduates and a further 37 percent and 34 percent had some college. These figures support the lesson's statement that the founding cohort was largely white, insured and comparatively well educated. Article is not open access; facts only.

title: Inside the Adverse Childhood Experience Score: Strengths, Limitations, and Misapplications (American Journal of Preventive Medicine 59(2), 293-295)
provider: Anda RF, Porter LE, Brown DW; Elsevier
license: Publisher records the article as hybrid open access under CC BY-NC-ND
notes: The publisher's full text was blocked to this session, and the PubMed record carries no abstract; the abstract was read from the publisher's abstract record retrieved through the Semantic Scholar API, and the citation was confirmed against PubMed (PMID 32222260). Supports: the ACE score is a relatively crude measure of cumulative childhood stress exposure that varies widely between people; unlike blood pressure or lipid levels it has no measurement reference standards or cut points for clinical decision making; the authors' concern that ACE scores are being misappropriated as a screening or diagnostic tool to infer individual risk and misapplied in treatment algorithms that assign population-based risk to individuals; and their call for ACE screening programs to be evaluated against USPSTF standards. Anda is a founding ACE Study investigator, which is why this commentary carries weight. Because only the abstract was accessible, the lesson attributes to this source only what the abstract states.

title: Curricular Alignment: A Re-Examination
provider: Lorin W. Anderson, University of South Carolina; Theory Into Practice 41(4), Autumn 2002 (College of Education, The Ohio State University); same scanned issue as the Krathwohl overview
notes: Article appearing later in the same scanned Theory Into Practice issue (deliberately given the same URL as the Krathwohl record, which is a scan of the whole issue). Supports the three-component alignment triangle (objectives/standards, instructional activities and materials, assessments) and the distinction between content coverage ('Is what we are teaching being tested?') and opportunity to learn ('Are we teaching what is being tested?'). Used only for that conceptual distinction; no wording reproduced.

title: Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct (2002, amended 2010 and 2016; effective January 1, 2017)
provider: American Psychological Association
notes: Source for the explicit aspirational-versus-enforceable distinction, the five General Principles, Standard 1.02 (conflicts between ethics and law) and 1.03 (conflicts between ethics and organizational demands), 2.01 boundaries of competence, 3.06 conflict of interest defined by impairment or exposure to harm, and 3.07 third-party requests for services and clarifying who the client is. Copyrighted; paraphrased only.

title: APA Resolution on Violent Video Games: February 2020 Revision to the 2015 Resolution
provider: American Psychological Association
notes: Professional-body policy document used for the current mainstream position and its explicit limits: an association with aggressive behavior, affect, and cognition and with reduced prosocial behavior, empathy, and moral engagement; the four meta-analytic effect sizes (0.19, 0.15, 0.08, 0.16) whose interpretations have varied dramatically; the statement that all violence is aggression but not all aggression is violence and that the literature has not focused on lethal violence; and the opening caution that the resolution should not be misused by attributing violence such as mass shootings to violent video game use. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced beyond short factual paraphrase.

title: The Paideia Proposal: An Educational Manifesto (catalogue record)
provider: Internet Archive (item metadata for the Macmillan edition)
notes: Bibliographic verification only, via the item metadata record: Mortimer Jerome Adler and the Paideia Group, The Paideia Proposal: An Educational Manifesto, New York: Macmillan, 1982. No content reproduced.

title: Existentialism in Education: What It Means (catalogue record)
provider: Internet Archive (item metadata for the Harper & Row edition)
notes: Bibliographic verification only: Van Cleve Morris, Existentialism in Education: What It Means, New York: Harper & Row, 1966. Used to date the introduction of existentialism into American teacher-education literature. No content reproduced.

title: The Theory and Practice of Culturally Relevant Education: A Synthesis of Research Across Content Areas (Review of Educational Research, 86(1), 163-206)
provider: Brittany Aronson (Miami University) and Judson Laughter (University of Tennessee, Knoxville); American Educational Research Association. Full text read from a publicly posted PDF copy.
notes: All 44 pages extracted and read. Used for Gay's definition of culturally responsive teaching as rendered from Gay (2010, p. 31) and for her six dimensions (p. 38), including academic empowerment through high expectations; for Ladson-Billings' three tenets and her 2006 clarification that the achievement criterion means student learning rather than standardized test scores; for the teaching-versus-pedagogy distinction between the two strands; for the confirmation that Ladson-Billings (2014) remixed her theory toward culturally sustaining pedagogy; for the method (four databases, 1995-2013, more than 40 studies synthesized across mathematics, science, social studies, English language arts, and English as a second language); and for the authors' own statements that the existing studies are small-scale, that the construct is not consistently defined across studies, that Morrison, Robbins and Rose found none of 45 classroom studies displaying all twelve identified culturally relevant actions, and that Lee found most English-learner work to be conceptual literature, program descriptions, and anecdotal calls. No wording reproduced.

title: Bandura, Ross, and Ross: Observational Learning and the Bobo Doll (ERIC ED499095)
provider: Anthony R. Artino, Jr., University of Connecticut; Education Resources Information Center (IES, U.S. Department of Education)
notes: Scholarly review used for the 1963 film-mediated follow-up (live, filmed human, and cartoon models against a control; exposure groups roughly twice as aggressive as controls, quoting the original at p. 9), for the four component subfunctions as stated in Bandura 1989, for the acquisition-versus-performance distinction and the three types of incentive motivator (direct, vicarious, self-produced), and for the intellectual context of Freudian catharsis and Skinnerian reinforcement that the studies argued against. Reuse terms not stated; used as reference only.

title: About ASC
provider: American Society of Criminology
notes: Read the page. The field's principal U.S. professional association describes its members as pursuing scholarly, scientific, and professional knowledge concerning the measurement, etiology, consequences, prevention, control, and treatment of crime and delinquency. Used to ground the definition of criminology as a research discipline distinct from the operating institutions of criminal justice.

title: Poverty Guidelines (2026 HHS poverty guidelines and explanatory notes)
provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation
license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
notes: Page retrieved and read in full as text. Supports the entire guidelines half of the three-way distinction: the 2026 guideline table for the 48 contiguous states and DC (one person $15,960 through eight persons $55,720, plus $5,680 for each additional person) and the separate Alaska and Hawaii tables; publication in the Federal Register in January 2026; the calculation method (2024 Census thresholds adjusted for 2024-to-2025 price change with rounding and uniform increments); the note that the 2026 guidelines compare the eleven available 2025 CPI-U months, October 2025 having been lost to the federal shutdown, with all twelve months of 2024; the statement that guidelines apply regardless of age while thresholds differ for householders 65 and older; the list of programmes that use the guidelines (Head Start, SNAP, National School Lunch, LIHEAP, CHIP) and those that do not (TANF, SSI, EITC); the Alaska and Hawaii differentiation tracing to Office of Economic Opportunity practice in 1966-1970 and the fact that thresholds have never had such figures; the statutory citation at 42 U.S.C. 9902(2); and the explicit warning that 'federal poverty level' is ambiguous and should be avoided where precision matters.

title: Effective Marginal Tax Rates / Benefit Cliffs
provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation
license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
notes: Page retrieved and read as text. Supports ASPE's definitions of the effective marginal tax rate (the portion of new earnings eroded by benefit reductions) and of a benefit cliff (a benefit reduction equal to or larger than the earnings increase that triggered it); the 2019 brief-series findings that the median marginal tax rate among households with children just above poverty was 51 percent, that only about 3 percent of CCDF households would lose their entire child care subsidy after a $2,000 earnings increase, and that about 7 percent of TANF households (roughly 100,000) faced marginal rates of 70 percent or more; and the existence of ASPE's 2024 study of how benefit recipients weigh benefit loss, the ease of resuming benefits once lost, and job instability when considering an earnings increase. Findings are reported as measured, with their 2019 date attached, and no policy position is taken.

title: Frequently Asked Questions Related to the Poverty Guidelines and Poverty
provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation
license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
notes: Read for the thresholds-versus-guidelines comparison. Supports which agency issues each measure, the statistical versus administrative purposes, the release timing (Census preliminary thresholds early in the calendar year and final thresholds in September; HHS guidelines in late January), the absence of geographic variation in thresholds against the separate Alaska and Hawaii guideline sets, the 48-cell threshold matrix versus the rounded uniform-increment guidelines, and the 1969 Bureau of the Budget designation of the thresholds as the official statistical definition of poverty.

title: Social Work Licensing Exams
provider: Association of Social Work Boards
notes: Source for the four examination categories (Bachelors, Masters, Advanced Generalist, Clinical), ASWB's role across United States and Canadian jurisdictions, and the sequence in which candidates apply to their state or provincial board before registering for an exam. Used to separate exam development from license granting. No licensure-eligibility guidance drawn from it.

title: Rules for licensure
provider: Association of Social Work Boards
notes: Source for the regulatory structure: statutes governing social work licensing are passed by state and provincial legislatures, those statutes empower boards to issue licenses and enforce practice standards, boards implement rules for practice, and social workers are required to abide by their board's standards of conduct in addition to the profession's code. Also supports that licensure requirements include an accredited degree, examination, and jurisdiction-set character requirements, and that ASWB links to every state and province's own statutes and rules. The related overview page at https://www.aswb.org/licenses/ states that every state and province has its own requirements for getting a license; that page was checked on the same date.

title: From short-term store to multicomponent working memory: The role of the modal model (Memory and Cognition, 47(4), 575-588)
provider: Alan D. Baddeley, Graham J. Hitch, Richard J. Allen; author accepted manuscript, White Rose Research Online
notes: Used for the description of the Atkinson and Shiffrin modal model and its components, for the development of the short-term store concept into the multicomponent working memory framework, and for the fact that proposals to replace short-term storage with activated long-term memory are current and contested.

title: Population vs Individual Prediction of Poor Health From Results of Adverse Childhood Experiences Screening (JAMA Pediatrics, 175(4), 385-393)
provider: Baldwin, Caspi, Meehan, Ambler, Arseneault, Fisher, Harrington, Matthews, Odgers, Poulton, Ramrakha, Moffitt, Danese / American Medical Association, open access via PubMed Central
notes: Abstract with full results verified through Europe PMC (PMID 33492366). Supports: ACE scores associated with later mental and physical health problems in the E-Risk and Dunedin cohorts (relative risks 1.14 and 1.09 per additional ACE in E-Risk) yet with poor individual predictive accuracy (AUC 0.58 for any mental health problem, 0.60 for any physical health problem, against 0.50 for chance), and the authors' conclusion that targeting interventions by ACE screening is likely to be ineffective. Used to support the anti-determinism rigor requirement.

title: Population vs Individual Prediction of Poor Health From Results of Adverse Childhood Experiences Screening (JAMA Pediatrics 175(4), 385-393)
provider: Baldwin JR, Caspi A, Meehan AJ, Ambler A, Arseneault L, Fisher HL, Harrington H, Matthews T, Odgers CL, Poulton R, Ramrakha S, Moffitt TE, Danese A; American Medical Association
license: CC BY
notes: Full text read on PubMed Central (PMC7835926). Supports the quantitative core of the ACE-misuse correction: in the E-Risk cohort (2,009 analyzed, followed to age 18) and the Dunedin cohort (918 analyzed, followed to age 45), ACE scores predicted mean group differences in health (relative risk 1.14 per additional ACE for any mental health problem, 1.09 for any physical health problem) but had poor individual accuracy, with areas under the curve of 0.58 and 0.60 against 0.50 for chance; the authors conclude that targeting interventions on the basis of ACE screening is likely to be ineffective at preventing poor health outcomes. Findings reported in the lesson's own wording.

title: Transmission of Aggression Through Imitation of Aggressive Models (Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63, 575-582)
provider: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila A. Ross; reproduced by Classics in the History of Psychology, York University
notes: Primary source for the 1961 design and results: 72 Stanford University Nursery School children aged 37-69 months (mean 52), three conditions of 24 with model sex counterbalanced, the mild aggression-arousal procedure, the imitative / partially imitative / nonimitative response categories, the sex differences, the inhibitory effect of the nonaggressive model, and the authors' own statistical cautions. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

title: Infants' performance in spontaneous-response false belief tasks: A review and meta-analysis (Infant Behavior and Development, 57, 101350)
provider: Barone, P., Corradi, G., & Gomila, A.; abstract record in PubMed (PMID 31445431)
notes: Abstract-level record (DOI 10.1016/j.infbeh.2019.101350) retrieved through the Europe PMC REST API; the full text is paywalled, so only findings stated in the abstract are used. Supports: 56 false-belief conditions from violation-of-expectation, anticipatory-looking, and interactive paradigms, covering 1,469 infants under two years; correct performance about 1.76 times more likely than incorrect performance; later publication year associated with weaker performance; the advantage concentrated in the violation-of-expectation paradigm; high heterogeneity and an asymmetric funnel plot indicating unpublished small-effect studies; and the authors' conclusion casting doubt on the robustness of the phenomenon. No wording reproduced.

title: Using Crisis Theory in Dealing With Severe Mental Illness - A Step Toward Normalization? (Frontiers in Sociology, 7, 805604, 2022)
provider: Baumgardt J, Weinmann S; PubMed Central (PMC9218753)
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: DOI 10.3389/fsoc.2022.805604. Full text read. Supports the lesson's account of crisis as a temporal and episodic phenomenon rather than a chronic, biologically driven condition; the framing of a crisis as a possible turning point; the observation that a crisis framing is less prone to medicalization than a diagnostic framing; and the caution that crisis theory was developed with people without severe mental illness in mind and needs modification before it is applied to that population.

title: Developmental Improvements and Persisting Difficulties in Children's Metacognitive Monitoring and Control Skills: Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Perspectives (Child Development, 92(4), 1502-1519)
provider: Bayard, N. S., van Loon, M. H., Steiner, M., & Roebers, C. M.; PubMed Central (PMC8248442)
license: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution License, as recorded for the article in Europe PMC)
notes: Open-access longitudinal and cross-sectional study (DOI 10.1111/cdev.13486) of 7-to-8-year-olds and 9-to-10-year-olds (longitudinal N = 305; cross-sectional comparison sample N = 144) on a paired-associate learning task administered twice a year apart. Used for the findings that retrospective monitoring and control (confidence judgments and withdrawal of answers) improved with age while prospective monitoring and control (judgments of learning and restudy selections) did not, that control remained suboptimal apparently because monitoring was overoptimistic, and that improvement in retrospective monitoring was attributable mainly to development rather than task familiarity. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

title: Trilogies: Lessons from 50 Years Facilitating Community-based Health Assessments and Planning in Appalachia
provider: Behringer B; Journal of Appalachian Health 6(1-2):149-163, East Tennessee State University
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Full text read via the Europe PMC REST API. Supports the working descriptions of Rothman's three strategies (locality development, social planning, social action) and their use as a strategy-selection device by community groups; the article cites Rothman's Planning and Organizing for Social Change (Columbia University Press, 1974) as the source of the trilogy. Also supports the observation that groups arrive with favoured strategies before comparing options. Facts synthesised; no wording reused.

title: Formative Assessment: A Critical Review (Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice, 18(1), 5-25)
provider: Randy Elliot Bennett; ERIC record EJ912798, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
notes: ERIC record consulted for the abstract. Supports the conclusions that 'formative assessment' does not yet represent a well-defined set of artefacts or practices, that the breadth of current definitions permits implementations with widely varying outcomes, and that the magnitude of commonly made quantitative effectiveness claims is suspect because it derives from untraceable, flawed, dated or unpublished sources.

title: How to Engage in Pseudoscience with Real Data: A Criticism of John Hattie's Arguments in 'Visible Learning' from the Perspective of a Statistician (McGill Journal of Education, 52(1))
provider: Pierre-Jerome Bergeron, University of Ottawa; translated by Lysanne Rivard; McGill Journal of Education
notes: Full text of the English translation downloaded from the journal and text-extracted, with the catalogue record confirmed through the ERIC API (EJ1150889). Used for the specific criticisms this lesson reports: that the common language effect values in Visible Learning can fall outside the range of a probability, a calculation error first flagged by Topphol in 2012; that Cohen's d cannot serve as a unit-free universal measure permitting comparison across arbitrarily different studies; that Hattie aggregates incommensurable effects under single labels; and that the choice of baseline comparison determines the sign of an effect, so a negative value need not mean a reverse effect. The article page states journal copyright with no Creative Commons licence, so it is reference only and no wording was reproduced.

title: Cultural Relevance at Scale: The Effects of an Ethnic Studies Expansion on Academic Outcomes (American Educational Research Journal, 2026; EdWorkingPapers AI26-1446, April 2026)
provider: Biraj Bisht, Sade Bonilla, Grace (Ha Eun) Kim, Emily K. Penner; Annenberg Institute at Brown University (EdWorkingPapers)
notes: Working-paper summary page read. Used for the district-wide expansion study design (student-level two-way fixed effects on 24,246 students in grades 6-12 in San Francisco Unified School District across 2007-08 through 2022-23), for the reported GPA increase of 0.17 grade points (0.24 standard deviations) and 5.6 percentage point reduction in course failure, and for the authors' statement that the expansion effects are comparable in magnitude to the earlier pilot. Cited in the lesson as a recent at-scale replication for a specific course, not as evidence for the general instructional approach. No wording reproduced.

title: Body-Worn Cameras in Law Enforcement Agencies, 2016 (NCJ 251775, November 2018)
provider: Shelley S. Hyland, Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Bulletin PDF read; data are from the 2016 LEMAS Body-Worn Camera Supplement, administered for the first time in 2016. Used for the 2016 acquisition rate (47% of 15,328 general-purpose agencies), the share of adopting agencies with a formal BWC policy (about 86%), and the four most common stated reasons for acquisition (about 80% each). U.S. government work; paraphrased only.

title: Contacts Between Police and the Public, 2022 (NCJ 308847)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the BJS report PDF (October 2024, Tapp and Davis), based on the 2022 Police-Public Contact Survey supplement to the NCVS. Source for the 2022 figures used in the lesson: 19 percent of U.S. residents age 16 or older (about 49.2 million) had police contact in the prior 12 months; 7.6 percent police-initiated, 11.2 percent resident-initiated, 2.5 percent traffic-accident related; among people whose most recent contact was police-initiated, 58 percent were drivers in traffic stops; among resident-initiated contacts, 46 percent were to report a possible crime.

title: Correctional Populations in the United States, 2022 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 308699)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the BJS publication landing page and highlights, published May 2024. Supports the yearend-2022 correctional totals used to show that incarceration is not the whole of corrections: 5,496,400 adults under correctional supervision, of whom 3,668,800 were on probation or parole and 1,827,600 were incarcerated.

title: Correctional Populations in the United States, 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 310413)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the full PDF (26 pages, published September 2025). The single source that lets institutional and community corrections be compared on the same basis at yearend 2023: total under correctional supervision 5,530,300 (BJS's published total, which adjusts for overlap between statuses); 3,772,000 under community supervision, comprising 3,103,400 on probation and 680,400 on parole; 1,852,900 incarcerated in prisons or local jails; a supervision rate of 2,100 per 100,000 adult residents, or 1 in 48 adults.

title: Criminal Victimization, 2023 (NCJ 309335)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the bulletin PDF (https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/cv23.pdf), September 2024, revised June 9, 2025; text extracted locally. Supports the National Crime Victimization Survey reporting-to-police figures for 2023 in table 4: 44.7% of violent victimizations, 29.9% of property victimizations, and 42.7% of burglary/trespassing victimizations reported to police; also the 2023 violent victimization rate of 22.5 per 1,000 persons age 12 or older.

title: Census of State and Local Law Enforcement Agencies, 2018 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 302187)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the BJS publication landing page and highlights, published October 2022. Supports the count used in the lesson: in June 2018, 17,541 state and local agencies performed law enforcement functions in the United States, of which local police departments were 67% and sheriffs' offices 17%.

title: Federal Justice Statistics, 2023 (NCJ 309946)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the BJS publication landing page and its highlights, published March 2025. Supports the federal-scale figure used for the federalism contrast: 94,411 suspects were arrested by federal law enforcement and booked by the U.S. Marshals Service in fiscal year 2023, and U.S. attorneys prosecuted 61% of suspects in matters concluded that year.

title: Federal Law Enforcement Officers, 2020 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 304752)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Supports the federal law enforcement layer: 136,815 full-time officers with arrest and firearm authority across 90 agencies in fiscal year 2020, with DHS and its Office of Inspector General accounting for 49% (66,410). Used only to size the federal layer against the state and local one; the lesson does not describe individual federal agencies' jurisdictions.

title: Jail Inmates in 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 309965)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the full PDF (35 pages, published April 2025). Supports the jail figures and definitions: 664,200 people in local jail custody at midyear 2023; 70% (467,600) unconvicted and 30% (196,600) convicted; average 32 days in custody before release from July 2022 to June 2023; the BJS definition of a jail as a facility generally operated under the authority of a sheriff, police chief, or county or city administrator, holding people before and after arraignment usually beyond 72 hours and those sentenced to 1 year or less; the 2,848 jail jurisdictions in the 2023 Annual Survey of Jails frame; and the exclusion of the six combined jail-prison states.

title: The Justice System
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: BJS's own description of case flow. Supports two claims the lesson makes: that there is no single U.S. criminal justice system but many similar, individually unique ones, with the response to crime mainly a state and local function; and that discretion operates at every stage, with police, prosecutors, judges, correctional officials, and paroling authorities each holding a distinct decision, subject to limits that vary by jurisdiction. Used for the handoff and discretion structure only - criminal-justice-system:what-is-criminal-justice owns the system framing and the attrition funnel.

title: Local Police Departments: Policies and Procedures, 2016 (NCJ 254826, August 2020)
provider: Connor Brooks, Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Statistical brief PDF read; data are from the 2016 Law Enforcement Management and Administrative Statistics survey. Used for Table 4 (share of local police departments with written policies or procedural directives, and the corresponding share of officers, for motor-vehicle stops 84.8/95.6, racial profiling or unbiased policing 81.5/95.1, stop and frisk 71.3/85.7, body-worn cameras 47.7/65.6, investigation of employee misconduct 88.4/98.1) and Table 8 (share requiring external investigation of firearm discharges and of uses of force resulting in death, with BJS's note that the question excluded civilian reviews). U.S. government work; paraphrased only.

title: Prisoners in 2023 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 310197)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the full PDF (47 pages, published September 2025). Supports the prison figures and definitions: 1,254,224 people under state or federal prison jurisdiction at yearend 2023, of whom Table 2 gives 1,097,597 state and 156,627 federal; 96% (1,210,300) sentenced to more than 1 year; the BJS definition of a prison as a long-term facility run by a state or the federal government typically holding people with sentences of more than 1 year, with sentence length varying by state; and the list of six states operating integrated prison-jail systems.

title: Prosecutors in State Courts, 2007 - Statistical Tables (NCJ 234211)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the PDF directly (12 pages, published December 2011); this is the URL that resolved, and it is the most recent BJS national census of state court prosecutors. Supports the structural claims only: prosecutors serve in the executive branch of state government, are afforded broad discretion by law over who is charged and whether a case goes to trial, and the chief prosecutor is answerable to the public as an elected or appointed official under titles that vary by state. The 2,330 office count is given in the lesson with its 2007 date. The report's caseload and budget figures are too old to present as current and are not used.

title: Sheriffs' Offices, 2016: Personnel (NCJ 252834)
provider: Bureau of Justice Statistics, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Read the full bulletin PDF. Supports two points: sheriffs' offices made up 20% (3,012) of the 15,322 general-purpose agencies and employed 25% (173,000) of their 701,000 full-time sworn officers as of June 30, 2016; and BJS's definition of general-purpose agencies expressly excludes sheriffs' offices with only jail and court duties, which establishes that some sheriffs' offices are custodial and court-serving rather than patrol agencies.

title: Inside the Black Box: Raising Standards Through Classroom Assessment (Phi Delta Kappan, 80(2), 1998)
provider: Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam; republished by Kappan Online, Phi Delta Kappa International
notes: Publisher republication consulted for the origin of the widely quoted effect-size range ('typical effect sizes of the formative assessment experiments were between 0.4 and 0.7', described as larger than most found for educational interventions), the claim that improved formative assessment helps low achievers more, the definition of formative work as evidence actually used to adapt teaching, and the statements that pupils given only marks or grades do not benefit from the feedback and that guidance should preferably come without overall marks. Cited as a historical claim, not as settled quantitative evidence.

title: Community Health Workers, Occupational Outlook Handbook
provider: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Department of Labor
notes: Source for community health workers as a third distinct occupation: 65,100 jobs in 2024, $51,030 May 2024 median wage, high school diploma typical entry, 11 percent projected growth 2024-34, outreach and care-coordination duties, and the community health representative / promotores de la salud / peer support specialist title variants. Read via an Internet Archive snapshot dated 2026-07-23. Public domain text; nothing quoted.

title: Social and Human Service Assistants, Occupational Outlook Handbook
provider: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Department of Labor
notes: Source for the distinct human-services occupation: 449,600 jobs in 2024, $45,120 May 2024 median wage, high school diploma typical entry, short-term on-the-job training, supervision by social workers and psychologists, alternate job titles, and the populations served. Read via an Internet Archive snapshot dated 2026-06-13 because BLS blocks automated retrieval. Public domain text; nothing quoted.

title: Social Workers, Occupational Outlook Handbook
provider: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Department of Labor
notes: Primary source for duties, practice settings, the four detailed social work occupations and their 2024 employment counts, May 2024 median wages, 2024-34 projections, largest employing industries, BSW/MSW education pathway, clinical licensure structure, state variation in titles, and the clinical-versus-macro distinction. BLS text and tables are public domain with credit requested; BLS usage policy prohibits automated retrieval, so the page was read via an Internet Archive snapshot dated 2026-06-11 of the same public page. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

title: Loss, trauma, and human resilience: have we underestimated the human capacity to thrive after extremely aversive events? (American Psychologist, 59(1), 20-28)
provider: George A. Bonanno / American Psychological Association
notes: Abstract verified through Europe PMC (PMID 14736317). Supports: many people exposed to loss or potentially traumatic events show only minor and transient disruptions in functioning; resilience is a distinct trajectory from recovery; resilience is more common than often believed; and the field underestimated it because its evidence came from people who sought treatment or showed great distress. Full text not retrieved and nothing reproduced.

title: Ethnic studies increases longer-run academic engagement and attainment (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 118(37), e2026386118)
provider: Sade Bonilla, Thomas S. Dee, Emily K. Penner; National Academy of Sciences, read via PubMed Central (PMC8449416)
notes: Used for the preregistered regression discontinuity design on students near a 2.0 eighth-grade GPA threshold in San Francisco Unified School District; for the sample of 1,405 students across five cohorts (2011-2014) at three high schools, described as lower-performing and more likely to have disabilities than the district generally; for the estimated increase in high school graduation of roughly 16 to 19 percentage points; for the suggestive but not conventionally significant postsecondary enrollment estimates of 10 to 16 percentage points; and for the authors' caveat that the results apply primarily to academically at-risk students near the threshold and may not generalize to higher-performing students. No wording reproduced.

title: The generalizability of the psychoanalytic concept of the working alliance (Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice, 16(3), 252-260)
provider: Edward S. Bordin / American Psychological Association
notes: Origin article for the pantheoretical working alliance. Author, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and 1979 date verified against the Crossref record for DOI 10.1037/h0085885. Full text paywalled; the three components (agreement on goals, consensus on tasks, bond) and the claim that different therapies place different demands on the relationship are taken from the summary of Bordin's position in Flueckiger et al. (2018), which is cited alongside it. No wording reproduced.

title: Getting help from 2-1-1: A statewide study of referral outcomes
provider: Boyum S, Kreuter MW, McQueen A, Thompson T, Greer R; Journal of Social Service Research 42(3):402-411; author manuscript on PubMed Central
notes: Full text read on PMC. The central referral-completion evidence in the lesson: random sample of 1,235 adult Missouri 2-1-1 callers followed at one month; 93 percent remembered referrals, 91 percent of those attempted contact, 82 percent of those reached a referral, 36 percent of those who reached one received assistance; reasons for non-assistance (agency had no funds 34 percent, caller did not qualify 25 percent); assistance by need (food 67, utilities 35, rent/mortgage 25, housing 17 percent); problem resolution roughly half at one month. Also supports the description of 211 resource databases containing eligibility information, application procedures and service locations for government, nonprofit and faith-based organizations, and the note that about half of 211s are operated through United Way. Data collected 2010-2012; used as dated evidence, not as a current national figure.

title: Critiquing and Analyzing the Effects of Neoliberalism on Community Organizing: Implications and Recommendations for Practitioners and Educators
provider: Brady SR, Schoeneman AC, Sawyer J; Journal for Social Action in Counseling and Psychology 6(1):36-60
license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (as stated on the journal article page)
notes: Full PDF read. Supports the historical placement of community organising's roots in the settlement house movement and Alinsky's pragmatic organising, the critique that professionalisation marginalises non-professional organisers, and the argument that dependence on government and large-foundation grants reduces a community organisation's autonomy over its mission. Treated as an attributed critical position. The no-derivatives licence means the record is REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording is reused.

title: Historical trauma among Indigenous Peoples of the Americas: concepts, research, and clinical considerations (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, 43(4), 282-290)
provider: Maria Yellow Horse Brave Heart, Josephine Chase, Jennifer Elkins, Deborah B. Altschul / Taylor & Francis
notes: Abstract verified through Europe PMC (PMID 22400458). Supports: historical trauma as collective, intergenerational massive group trauma compounded by continuing discrimination, racism, and oppression; its association with unresolved grief; and the article's own caution that tribal, cultural, and regional differences shape how wounding across generations is experienced and addressed. Used to attribute the concept and to warn against applying it to individuals by group membership.

title: Prevalence of secondary traumatic stress among social workers (Social Work, 52(1), 63-70)
provider: Brian E. Bride / National Association of Social Workers, Oxford University Press
notes: Citation and abstract verified through the Europe PMC record. Supports: secondary traumatic stress framed as an occupational hazard of direct service with traumatized populations; the finding that direct-practice social workers are highly likely to be secondarily exposed to traumatic events through their work; that many are likely to experience at least some STS symptoms; and that a significant minority may meet diagnostic criteria for PTSD. Full text paywalled, so the lesson reports the abstract's qualitative findings and attaches no percentages beyond them.

title: Appropriate Criteria: Key to Effective Rubrics
provider: Susan M. Brookhart, Duquesne University; Frontiers in Education 3:22
license: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution License), stated in the article
notes: Full 12-page article downloaded and text-extracted. Supports the two-part definition of a rubric (criteria plus performance level descriptions), the separation of rubrics from checklists and rating scales, the general-versus-task-specific distinction, the analytic-versus-holistic purposes, the 'has three sources' versus 'uses a variety of relevant, credible sources' example of directions-as-criteria, and the review counts: 46 studies yielding 51 rubrics, 29 of 51 analytic descriptive, 7 of 51 using rating-scale language or counting occurrences, only 56 percent of studies reporting rubric use with students, no relationship between rubric type or quality and study results, and the author's own publication-bias caution. No passage reproduced despite the permissive licence.

title: Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association, 564 U.S. 786 (2011) (No. 08-1448), majority opinion
provider: Supreme Court of the United States (text checked on the Legal Information Institute mirror, Cornell Law School)
notes: U.S. Supreme Court majority opinion used only as evidence that the same psychological literature has been read very differently by a second authoritative reader: the Court characterized the research as nearly all correlational rather than causal, noted admitted methodological flaws, and described the demonstrated effects as small and not specific to violent video games. Federal judicial opinions are public domain; no legal advice is given in the lesson.

title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators
provider: Matthias Brunmair, Tobias Richter; Psychological Bulletin 145(11), 1029-1052, 2019; PubMed record 31556629
notes: Abstract verified through the NCBI E-utilities API. Supports the corpus (59 studies, 238 effect sizes, 158 samples), the overall effect (Hedges' g = 0.42), the material-specific effects (paintings 0.67, mathematics 0.34, words -0.39, texts and tastes non-significant), and the three similarity/complexity moderators.

title: Enhancing and Undermining Intrinsic Motivation: The Effects of Task-Involving and Ego-Involving Evaluation on Interest and Performance (British Journal of Educational Psychology, 58(1), 1-14)
provider: Ruth Butler; ERIC record EJ380489, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
notes: ERIC bibliographic record consulted; full text is behind a publisher paywall and was not read. Establishes the study's existence, design (fifth- and sixth-grade classes, three feedback conditions involving grades and individual comments) and framing in terms of task-involving versus ego-involving evaluation. The lesson's statement about grades blunting comments is carried jointly by this record, the Ohio State summary and Black and Wiliam; no numeric result from Butler is reported.

title: California Business and Professions Code section 729 - Sexual exploitation by physician and surgeon, psychotherapist, or alcohol and drug abuse counselor
provider: California Legislative Information, California Legislature
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Read for the proposition that some states criminalize sexual contact between practitioner and client: the section makes such contact a public offense for covered practitioners including psychotherapists and alcohol and drug abuse counselors, reaches former patients where the relationship was terminated primarily to engage in the conduct, provides that consent is not a defense, and grades a first offense involving one victim as a misdemeanor with felony exposure where there are multiple victims or a repeat offense. Used as an illustration, not as a statement of any other state's law.

title: California Civil Code section 3294 (exemplary damages)
provider: California Legislative Information (California Legislative Counsel)
license: State statutory text; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Section text read from the Legislature's own site. Used for subdivision (a): in an action for breach of an obligation not arising from contract, where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, the plaintiff may recover damages for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant, in addition to actual damages. Cited as a concrete instance of state variation and of the intermediate standard operating inside a civil case.

title: California Constitution, Article XI, Section 1
provider: California Legislative Counsel (official California Legislative Information)
license: California statutory and constitutional text published by the Legislative Counsel is not subject to copyright restriction on reproduction of the text itself
notes: Read the official text. Subdivision (b) requires the Legislature to provide for county powers, an elected county sheriff, an elected district attorney, an elected assessor, and an elected governing body in each county. Used as one verified state example so the lesson can illustrate county-level electoral accountability without generalizing to all fifty states, which the research did not check. No constitutional text is quoted in the lesson.

title: 2024 Court Statistics Report: Statewide Caseload Trends (Data for Figures 24-33, Criminal Filings, Dispositions, and Caseload Clearance Rate, FY 2013-14 through FY 2022-23)
provider: Judicial Council of California
notes: Official California superior court caseload series. Supplies the FY2022-23 filing counts for felonies, nontraffic and traffic misdemeanors, and nontraffic and traffic infractions used in the volume discussion. Percentages in the lesson were computed from these counts, not taken from the report.

title: California Penal Code section 1096 - Presumption of innocence and reasonable doubt
provider: California Legislative Information, California Legislature
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Read live (as amended by Stats. 1995, ch. 46). The defendant is presumed innocent; the effect of the presumption is to place on the state the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; reasonable doubt is defined as leaving jurors unable to say they feel an abiding conviction of the truth of the charge. Used to show how a state codifies the Winship standard.

title: California Penal Code section 198.5 - Residential presumption of reasonable fear
provider: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo)
notes: Supports the castle-doctrine presumption of reasonable fear of imminent peril of death or great bodily injury against a non-household member who unlawfully and forcibly enters a residence, where the resident knew or had reason to believe the entry occurred.

title: California Penal Code section 20 - Union of act and intent
provider: California Legislative Information, California Legislature
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Read live. The section, enacted in 1872 and still in force, provides that in every crime or public offense there must exist a union, or joint operation of act and intent, or criminal negligence. Used as a statutory illustration of the concurrence requirement in one state; not offered as the rule in any other jurisdiction.

title: California Penal Code section 26 - Persons capable of committing crimes
provider: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo)
notes: Supports the codified incapacity classes: children under 14 absent clear proof they knew the act's wrongfulness; persons who are mentally incapacitated; persons acting under ignorance or mistake of fact disproving criminal intent; unconsciousness; accident or misfortune without evil design or culpable negligence; and duress except for capital crimes.

title: California Penal Code section 270 - Parent's failure to provide for a minor child
provider: California Legislative Information, California Legislature
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Read live. A parent who wilfully omits, without lawful excuse, to furnish necessary clothing, food, shelter, medical attendance, or other remedial care for a minor child is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not exceeding $2,000, imprisonment in the county jail not exceeding one year, or both, with greater exposure after a judicial paternity adjudication. Used as a verified example of a status-relationship duty codified by statute, so that an omission can satisfy the act element; state law varies.

title: California Penal Code section 17 - Felony, misdemeanor, and infraction defined; alternative sentencing
provider: California Legislative Counsel (California Legislative Information)
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Subsections (a) and (b) read verbatim; primary authority for the wobbler mechanism and for California's residual definition of misdemeanor.

title: California Penal Code section 489 - Punishment for grand theft
provider: California Legislative Counsel (California Legislative Information)
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Subsection (c)(1) read verbatim: general grand theft is punishable by county jail not exceeding one year or pursuant to section 1170(h), which is what makes it a wobbler.

title: California Penal Code section 490.2 - Petty theft; obtaining property by theft where value does not exceed $950
provider: California Legislative Counsel (California Legislative Information)
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Establishes California's $950 petty-theft ceiling (added by Proposition 47 in 2014, amended by Proposition 63 in 2016), with narrow exceptions for firearms and specified prior convictions.

title: California Penal Code Sec. 835a - Use of force by peace officers
provider: California Legislative Information, California Legislature
notes: Read the current section text, which the page states was amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 241, sec. 24 (SB 857), effective January 1, 2026. Used as one worked example of how a state criminal-law standard differs from the federal constitutional minimum: deadly force is justified only when the officer reasonably believes, based on the totality of the circumstances, that it is necessary to defend against an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury or to apprehend a fleeing person for a felony that threatened or resulted in death or serious bodily injury where the officer reasonably believes the person will cause death or serious bodily injury unless immediately apprehended; the requirement, where feasible, of identification and a warning before deadly force; and the statutory definitions of deadly force, imminent, and totality of the circumstances. The lesson states that this is California law only and that state law varies.

title: Rufo v. Simpson, 86 Cal. App. 4th 573 (Cal. Ct. App. 2001)
provider: California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District, Division Four (opinion text read through an Internet Archive capture of the Justia rendering)
notes: Read because law.justia.com and courtlistener.com both blocked direct automated retrieval; the Internet Archive capture of 27 December 2023 was used instead, and the record is marked reference only for that reason even though the underlying opinion is a government edict. Used for: the statement that in a prior criminal trial Simpson was acquitted of the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman while in the civil trial the jury concluded he killed them, having acted willfully and wrongfully with oppression and malice; the awards of $8.5 million compensatory damages on the wrongful death cause of action and $12.5 million punitive damages on each of the two survival actions; the disposition affirming the judgments, decided 26 January 2001 with review denied 25 April 2001; the observation that the parties to the prior criminal proceeding were Simpson and the People of the State of California represented by the Los Angeles County District Attorney, and that none of the civil plaintiffs had been a party to it; and the court's restatement that the purposes of punitive damages under California law are to punish the defendant and deter similar acts. No wording from the page is reproduced.

title: Effects of Teachers' Praise-to-Reprimand Ratios on Elementary Students' On-Task Behaviour (Grantee Submission; ERIC ED606564; published in Educational Psychology 40(10))
provider: Paul Caldarella, Ross A. A. Larsen, Leslie Williams, Kade R. Downs, Howard P. Wills and Joseph H. Wehby; grantee submission to the Institute of Education Sciences, via ERIC
notes: Author manuscript downloaded from the ERIC full-text server and text-extracted, and the corresponding journal record (EJ1275006) verified through the ERIC API. Used for the study's scale - three years of data from 19 elementary schools and 151 classrooms across three states, collected during a multi-site efficacy trial - for the finding of a positive linear relationship between praise-to-reprimand ratio and student on-task behavior, and for the explicit finding that no threshold ratio such as 3:1 or 4:1 was identified at which behavior dramatically improved. No wording reproduced.

title: The volume and characteristics of insanity defense pleas: an eight-state study, Bulletin of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law 19(4):331-338 (1991)
provider: Callahan LA, Steadman HJ, McGreevy MA, Robbins PC; record via PubMed (National Library of Medicine)
notes: Bibliographic record and abstract retrieved through the NCBI E-utilities esearch and efetch APIs (PMID 1786413). Supports the two reported figures: the insanity defense was raised in about one percent of all felony cases across the eight study states, and about 26 percent of those raising it were acquitted not guilty by reason of insanity. Only the abstract's reported statistics are used; no article prose is reproduced, and the lesson dates and geographically bounds the numbers.

title: Book review: Principles of Preventive Psychiatry by Gerald Caplan (Mental Health (London), 24(4), 1965, p. 174)
provider: Guise-Moores S, National Association for Mental Health; PubMed Central (PMC5085475)
license: CC BY-NC 4.0
notes: Contemporaneous review confirming that Caplan's Principles of Preventive Psychiatry was published by Tavistock in 1964, that its approach drew on Lindemann's crisis theory, that it located helping leverage in people facing a developmental or accidental hazard involving loss, threat, or challenge where short-term intervention has maximum impact, and that a reader in 1965 already warned the framework might be accepted too uncritically and doubted whether crisis intervention's effects would outlast the crisis. Used for historical grounding and for the lesson's point that the critique is as old as the theory. Paraphrased; no wording reproduced.

title: Universal Design for Learning (What We Do)
provider: CAST, Inc.
notes: Read for CAST's framing of UDL as a framework grounded in what is known about the brain, for learner variability described as predictable rather than exceptional, for the mapping of the three principles onto why / what / how of learning (interest and persistence; perception, language, comprehension; physical action, communication, executive function), and for CAST's position that the environment rather than the learner should be adjusted. Plain copyright notice; no wording reproduced.

title: CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines (Version 3.0)
provider: CAST, Inc.
notes: Guidelines site read for the three organizing principles - designing multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression - and for CAST's framing of the guidelines as support for proactively designing goals, methods, materials, assessments and learning environments around learner variability. The site carries a plain CAST copyright notice with no open license, so it is reference only and no wording is reproduced. Used only for the brief contrast with differentiation; the inclusive-teaching topic owns UDL.

title: Distinguishing Formative Assessment from Other Educational Assessment Labels
provider: Formative Assessment for Students and Teachers (FAST) SCASS, Council of Chief State School Officers (2012); copy hosted by the Michigan Department of Education
notes: Read in full. Source for the 2006 FAST SCASS definition and its six attributes, and for the definitions and commentary on interim/benchmark, summative, diagnostic, curriculum-embedded, universal screening and progress-monitoring assessment; for the Heritage quotation about the false assumption that formative assessment is a measurement instrument; for the statement that no meaningful evidence had been found that interim assessments enhance student learning; and for the point that a curriculum-embedded assessment used for grading differs from other summative processes only in how it is blended into instruction. Copyright CCSSO with no open licence stated, so definitions are restated in original wording.

title: Revising the Definition of Formative Assessment
provider: Formative Assessment for Students and Teachers (FAST) State Collaborative on Assessment and Student Standards, Council of Chief State School Officers (2018); copy hosted by the Michigan Department of Education
license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the document: '(c) 2018 by CCSSO. Revising the Definition of Formative Assessment is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License')
notes: Read in full. Source for the 2006 original and 2018 revised FAST SCASS definitions, the five integrated practices, the explicit statement that defining formative assessment as a process was a direct counter to treating it as an instrument, the rationale for adding 'planned' and 'ongoing' including contingent planning, and the shift from 'instruction' to 'learning and teaching'. Licensed CC BY 4.0, so definitions are quoted with attribution.

title: About Adverse Childhood Experiences
provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Used only for prevalence context supporting the universal-precautions design argument: about 64 percent of U.S. adults reported at least one type of adverse childhood experience before age 18 and 17.3 percent reported four or more types. title: Poverty: The History of the Official Poverty Measure
provider: U.S. Census Bureau
license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
notes: Supports the origin story used in the lesson: Mollie Orshansky of the Social Security Administration developed the thresholds in the mid-1960s during the War on Poverty by taking the cost of a minimum food diet (the economy food plan) and multiplying by three to allow for all other expenses; the measure was subsequently fixed as the official federal statistical definition through OMB Statistical Policy Directive 14; and the Supplemental Poverty Measure was later developed to address limitations the official measure could not address.

title: National Experimental Well-Being Statistics (NEWS) Project

license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States

The P60-287 appendix confirms the release history (February 2023 for 2018, January 2025, and July 2025 extending coverage to 2016-2021).

title: Poverty in the United States: 2024 (Current Population Reports, P60-287)
provider: U.S. Census Bureau (Emily A. Shrider and Christina Bijou)
license: U.S. Government work; not subject to copyright in the United States
notes: Sixty-two-page report downloaded and read in full via local text extraction. The spine of the lesson. Supports: the 2024 official poverty rate of 10.6 percent and 35.9 million people; the 2024 SPM rate of 12.9 percent; the side-by-side 'Differences in Poverty Measures' table (measurement unit, threshold basis, threshold adjustments, updating method, resource measure, universe, time series); the official 2024 threshold matrix (four people with two related children, $31,812; weighted average for four people, $32,130); the statement that official thresholds do not vary geographically and are updated by CPI-U; the 2024 SPM two-adult two-child thresholds by tenure (owners with mortgage $39,068, owners without $32,586, renters $39,430, BLS research series finalised 23 April 2025); SPM rates by tenure (renters 23.3, owners without mortgage 11.7, owners with mortgage 6.1 percent); the official+ device; the 2024 SPM/official+ gap of 2.3 percentage points and the threshold-growth explanation (base SPM thresholds up 5.2-5.8 percent, official up 2.9 percent); the age gap driven by medical expenses (65+ SPM 15.0 vs official+ 9.9); the income-to-poverty distribution (5.0 percent below half the threshold under official+ vs 4.2 percent under SPM; 45.8 vs 22.7 percent at 4.00 or more); the element-by-element transfer analysis (Social Security 28.7 million and 8.5 percentage points, 20.1 million of them 65 and older; refundable tax credits 6.8 million including 3.7 million children; medical expenses pushing 7.5 million into poverty, 3.7 points for those 65 and older, 2.1 for children, 1.8 for 18-64) together with the Census Bureau's own caveat that the additions and subtractions are independent and assume no behavioural change; Table B-2 child SPM rates (2021 5.2 percent, 2022 12.4 percent, 2024 13.4 percent) and the report's attribution of the 2021 lows to pandemic-era policies aimed at families with children and of the 2022 rise to those policies ending; the Census Bureau's statement that thresholds are 'a statistical yardstick' rather than a full account of need; and the statement that the SPM is not designed for programme eligibility or funding distribution.

provider: Cerasoli, C. P., Nicklin, J. M., & Ford, M. T., Psychological Bulletin 140(4), 2014
