notes: Bibliographic verification of the fourth edition (Guilford Press, 2023, ISBN 9781462552795, 338 pages) and of chapter structure, which confirms the direction of the terminology changes - for example 'Planting Seeds' is a fourth-edition chapter title. Used for citation facts only.

title: Democracy and Education: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Education (1916)
provider: John Dewey, via Project Gutenberg
license: Public domain in the USA (Project Gutenberg record)
notes: Primary source. Full text checked directly for Dewey's technical definition of education as reconstruction or reorganization of experience, and for his sustained argument against dualisms in educational theory. Source of the lesson's single direct quotation.

title: The concept of boundaries in clinical practice: theoretical and risk-management dimensions
provider: Thomas G. Gutheil and Glen O. Gabbard; American Journal of Psychiatry 150(2):188-196
notes: Citation metadata and the published abstract retrieved through the NCBI E-utilities efetch API (PMID 8422069, DOI 10.1176/ajp.150.2.188). Source for the origin of the boundary crossing versus boundary violation distinction, the list of domains the authors examined (role, time, place and space, money, gifts and services, clothing, language, self-disclosure, physical contact), and their conclusion that the impact of a particular crossing can only be assessed in clinical context. Full text is paywalled and was not read; no wording reproduced.

title: Misuses and misunderstandings of boundary theory in clinical and regulatory settings
provider: Thomas G. Gutheil and Glen O. Gabbard; American Journal of Psychiatry 155(3):409-414
notes: Citation metadata and structured abstract retrieved through the NCBI E-utilities efetch API (PMID 9501754, DOI 10.1176/ajp.155.3.409). Source for the authors' own critique of how their 1993 framework was applied: that an overreaction occurred requiring correction, that excessive rigidity and defensive practice can degrade care, that state statutes had broadened definitions of sexual misconduct, and that boundaries should be treated as flexible standards of good practice rather than lists of generically forbidden behavior. Full text paywalled; no wording reproduced.

title: Cultural Ways of Learning: Individual Traits or Repertoires of Practice (Educational Researcher, 32(5), 19-25)
provider: Kris D. Gutierrez and Barbara Rogoff; American Educational Research Association. Full text read from a publicly posted PDF copy hosted by the Laboratory of Comparative Human Cognition, University of California San Diego.
notes: Full text extracted and read. Used for the argument against treating cultural regularities as static traits attributable categorically to ethnic group membership; for the definition of linguistic and cultural-historical repertoires as ways of engaging in activity stemming from observing and participating in cultural practices; for the point that an important feature of a repertoire focus is helping people develop dexterity in choosing which approach fits which circumstance; for the statement that trait approaches encourage overgeneralization, treat groups as homogeneous with fixed characteristics, and have yielded a kind of tracking in which instruction is adjusted merely on a group categorization; for the observation that many learning- and cognitive-style typologies are offered as categories without research substantiating their relationship to the groups characterized; and for their citation of Tiedeman that the evidence is inadequate to judge cognitive styles' validity or usefulness for adapting instruction. No wording reproduced.

title: Ceremonial Justice: Crime and Punishment in a Loosely Coupled System, Social Forces 58(2):506 (1979)
provider: John Hagan, John D. Hewitt, and Duane F. Alwin / Social Forces
notes: Bibliographic record verified through the Crossref API only (authors Hagan, Hewitt, Alwin; Social Forces, vol. 58, iss. 2, p. 506, December 1979). Full text is paywalled and was NOT retrieved, and Crossref carries no abstract. Cited in this lesson for one narrow purpose that the article's own title establishes: that criminologists were analyzing criminal punishment as operating in a 'loosely coupled system' by 1979. No claim about the article's findings is made.

title: How Long Does It Take English Learners to Attain Proficiency? (Policy Report 2000-1)
provider: Kenji Hakuta, Yuko Goto Butler, Daria Witt; University of California Linguistic Minority Research Institute; Education Resources Information Center (ERIC ED443275), IES, U.S. Department of Education
notes: ERIC record and abstract read for the finding that, in districts considered most successful at teaching English to limited-English-proficient students, oral proficiency took 3 to 5 years to develop and academic English proficiency 4 to 7 years; for the study base of four districts (two California, two Canada); and for the authors' conclusion that policies assuming rapid acquisition, including one-year sheltered English programs, are unrealistic. Used for the conversational-versus-academic-language distinction. The lesson presents these as estimates from this study rather than as universal constants.

title: Trauma informed interventions: A systematic review (PLoS ONE 16(6): e0252747)
provider: Han HR, Miller HN, Nkimbeng M, Budhathoki C, Mikhael T, Rivers E, Gray J, Trimble K, Chow S, Wilson P; Public Library of Science
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC record (PMC8219147). Supports the point that the trauma-informed label is applied inconsistently: of 32 studies, most tested established psychotherapies delivered by medical professionals in outpatient settings, with EMDR and CBT the most common, and the authors concluded that evidence for psychological outcomes is inconsistent. Used to explain why systematic reviews of this field cannot pool their results.

title: Functional Analysis of Problem Behavior: A Review (Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 36(2), 147-185)
provider: Gregory P. Hanley, Brian A. Iwata and Brandon E. McCord; Society for the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, via PubMed Central
notes: Read on PubMed Central. Used only for the review's classification of the variables that maintain problem behavior - social positive reinforcement (attention, access to tangible items), social negative reinforcement (escape or avoidance), and automatic or nonsocial reinforcement - and for the fact that functional analysis has become a standard component of contemporary behavioral assessment. The lesson does not teach functional analysis methodology. Publisher copyright; no wording reproduced.

title: Toxic Stress (Key Concepts)
provider: Center on the Developing Child, Harvard University
notes: Verified the positive, tolerable, and toxic stress response definitions and the role of supportive, responsive adult relationships in buffering; the page credits the National Scientific Council on the Developing Child's work. Page carries a Harvard copyright notice, so no wording reproduced; the lesson attributes the framing and restates it.

title: Human Behavior and the Social Environment I - The Person in Environment
provider: Susan Tyler, University of Arkansas Pressbooks (2020)
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
notes: Open social work text (licence shown on the page). Read in full. Corroborates the standard undergraduate treatment: person-in-environment as an orienting approach, micro/mezzo/macro levels, systems theory, ecological theory including the role of the client's own perception of their situation, and Bronfenbrenner's five levels. NC-SA terms are incompatible with reuse here, so it was used only to check that this lesson matches how the concept is actually taught; no wording adapted.

title: Social Determinants of Health - Healthy People 2030
provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion
notes: Federal health objectives. Verified directly: SDOH defined as the conditions in the environments where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship and age that affect health, functioning and quality-of-life outcomes and risks; grouped into five domains (Economic Stability; Education Access and Quality; Health Care Access and Quality; Neighborhood and Built Environment; Social and Community Context); one of five overarching goals targets social, physical and economic environments; page states plainly that promoting healthy choices alone will not eliminate disparities and emphasises 'upstream' factors usually unrelated to health care delivery. Facts synthesised; no prose adapted.

title: A Model of Learning Objectives based on A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives
provider: Rex Heer, Center for Excellence in Learning and Teaching, Iowa State University (updated January 2012); copy hosted by the University of Central Florida Office of Effectiveness and Accreditation Support
license: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported
notes: Widely used two-dimensional model of the revised taxonomy, with the license statement printed on the document itself. Supports the verb-plus-object structure of an objective (the verb names the intended cognitive process, the object names the knowledge to be acquired or constructed) and the document's own caveat that the distinctions between categories are not always clear-cut - an objective involving analysing or evaluating may demand thinking no less complex than one involving creating. Its verb and knowledge-type tables were NOT reproduced; all verb examples in the lesson are original.

title: Administrative Burden: Policymaking by Other Means (2018)
provider: Pamela Herd and Donald P. Moynihan; Russell Sage Foundation (publisher's book page)
notes: Publisher's book page read for accurate attribution: authors, title, publisher and December 2018 publication, and the publisher's summary that administrative burdens are the result of deliberate policy choices rather than unintended byproducts, and that they fall hardest on people least able to absorb their financial and psychological costs. The book is copyrighted; the learning / compliance / psychological cost taxonomy is described in original wording, attributed to the authors, and marked as their argument. The Tier A anchor for the same three categories is OMB M-22-10.

title: Motivational interviewing
provider: Annual Review of Clinical Psychology, 1, 91-111 (Hettema, Steele, Miller)
notes: Meta-analysis of 72 trials; source for the short-term effect size of 0.77 decaying to 0.30 at one year and for the statement that effectiveness is highly variable across providers, populations, target problems, and settings.

title: National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) in Health and Health Care
provider: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health (Think Cultural Health)
notes: Supports Standards 5-8: language assistance offered at no cost to the individual, notice that it is available, verification of the competence of those providing it with untrained individuals and minors avoided and discouraged as interpreters, and easy-to-understand materials and signage. Rights not separately verified on the page, so treated as reference only.

title: Scaffolding and Achievement in Problem-Based and Inquiry Learning: A Response to Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark (2006)
provider: Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Duncan, R. G., & Chinn, C. A.; Educational Psychologist 42(2), 99-107 (2007); ERIC EJ772220
notes: Full text read from a university course copy (Simon Fraser University), with the abstract and bibliographic record confirmed through ERIC and Crossref (DOI 10.1080/00461520701263368). Used for the conflation argument, for the statement that all learning involves knowledge construction and is therefore a constructivist process, for the description of problem-based and inquiry learning as extensively scaffolded, and for the reported Dochy et al. meta-analytic pattern of no effect on declarative knowledge with a moderate effect favoring PBL on knowledge application. No prose reproduced.

title: Effect of crisis resolution team treatment on crisis experience and crisis coping: a multicenter pre-post study in Norway (BMC Psychiatry, 25(1), 1067, 2025)
provider: Holgersen KH, Hasselberg N, Siqveland J, Ruud T; PubMed Central (PMC12593888)
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: DOI 10.1186/s12888-025-07491-y. Full text read. Supports the working definition used in the lesson - crises described in both the disaster literature and the crisis-team literature as ordinary human reactions to severe psychosocial stressors, or situations where a person is overwhelmed and usual coping breaks down - and the statement that general crisis theory underpins the development of crisis resolution teams while little research has examined what actually happens in these contacts. The article's dating of Lindemann and Caplan is transposed and was not relied on.

title: Cultural Humility: Measuring Openness to Culturally Diverse Clients (Journal of Counseling Psychology, 60(3), 353-366)
provider: Joshua N. Hook, Don E. Davis, Jesse Owen, Everett L. Worthington Jr. and Shawn O. Utsey; American Psychological Association. Bibliographic record and abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 23647387).
notes: Supports: the definition of cultural humility as an other-oriented rather than self-focused interpersonal stance characterised by respect and a lack of superiority toward a person's cultural background and experience; the development across four studies of a client-rated measure of a therapist's cultural humility; and the finding that clients' perceptions of their therapist's cultural humility were positively associated with a strong working alliance and with improvement in therapy, with the alliance mediating that relationship. Cited in the lesson as correlational, measurement-based evidence, which is what the abstract reports. Abstract only; no full text read and no wording reproduced.

title: Student Motivation and Associated Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis From Self-Determination Theory
provider: Howard, J. L., Bureau, J., Guay, F., Chong, J. X. Y., & Ryan, R. M., Perspectives on Psychological Science 16(6), 2021
notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API (PMID 33593153). Source of the 344 samples / 223,209 participants figure and of the differential profile of intrinsic, identified, introjected, external regulation and amotivation across performance, persistence and well-being outcomes.

title: Explicit Instruction: Historical and Contemporary Contexts (Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 32(3), 140-148)
provider: Charles A. Hughes, Jared R. Morris, William J. Therrien, Sarah K. Benson; ERIC record EJ1150825
notes: Abstract retrieved through the ERIC API and bibliographic details confirmed (DOI 10.1111/ldrp.12142). Used for the central definitional point of this lesson: that explicit instruction is not a unitary intervention but a combination of over a dozen teaching behaviours used to design and deliver instruction, that this multicomponent character explains why published definitions disagree, and that the term must be distinguished from earlier 'Direct Instruction' programs and 'direct instruction' research. Abstract-level verification only; no wording reproduced.

title: A meta-analytic review of achievement goal measures: different labels for the same constructs or different constructs with similar labels?
provider: Hulleman, C. S., Schrager, S. M., Bodmann, S. M., & Harackiewicz, J. M., Psychological Bulletin 136(3), 2010
notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API (PMID 20438145). Source of the 243 studies / 91,087 participants figure, the r = .14 versus r = -.14 contrast for normatively referenced versus appearance-and-evaluative performance-approach scales, the mastery-approach goal-relevant-language contrast, and the conclusion that the same label is applied to conceptually different constructs.

title: Promoting interest and performance in high school science classes
provider: Hulleman, C. S., & Harackiewicz, J. M., Science 326(5958), 1410-1412, 2009
notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API (PMID 19965759). Used for the worked example: a randomized field experiment in which encouraging high school students to connect course material to their lives increased interest in science and course grades for students with low expectations of success.

title: What's Wrong With Madeline Hunter? (Educational Leadership, February 1985)
provider: Madeline Hunter, Graduate School of Education, University of California, Los Angeles; ASCD
notes: Hunter's own five-page response to critics, downloaded and text-extracted (scanned original; OCR is imperfect but the relevant passages are legible). Used as the primary source for her framing of the model as a clinical theory of instruction premised on the teacher as decision maker, for her statement that her purpose was to tell teachers what to consider before deciding what to do, for the 'white sauce recipe' passage rejecting the expectation that every element appear in every lesson, for the statement that an observer using a checklist to confirm all seven elements does not understand the model, and for her standard that models are judged on guiding behavior, predicting outcomes and stimulating research rather than on being the final answer. No reuse license stated.

title: The strengths based approach as a service delivery model for severe mental illness: a meta-analysis of clinical trials (BMC Psychiatry, 14:243)
provider: Ibrahim, N., Michail, M., & Callaghan, P. / BMC Psychiatry
license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)
notes: Open-access meta-analysis. Supports the lesson's evidence paragraph: five studies pooled (four RCTs, one quasi-experimental), 194 participants, no significant effect on level of functioning or quality of life, moderate-quality evidence, low trial count, and explicit criticism of unclear randomization/blinding, heterogeneous measures, and the lack of clear description of the underlying intervention. Findings restated in original wording; no text reproduced.

title: 20 U.S.C. 1400(d) - Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, Purposes
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA statute site)
notes: Statutory text of IDEA's purposes. Used for the lesson's framing of what the statute is for, specifically 1400(d)(1)(A): ensuring that all children with disabilities have available to them a free appropriate public education emphasizing special education and related services designed to meet their unique needs and prepare them for further education, employment, and independent living. U.S. statutory text is a government edict and is not copyrightable.

title: IDEA Sec. 1412(a)(5) - Least restrictive environment
provider: U.S. Department of Education, IDEA statute site (Office of Special Education Programs)
notes: Federal statutory text read for subparagraph (A): to the maximum extent appropriate, children with disabilities are educated with children who are not disabled, and special classes, separate schooling, or other removal from the regular educational environment occurs only when the nature or severity of the disability is such that education in regular classes with the use of supplementary aids and services cannot be achieved satisfactorily. Used to support the claim that federal law conditions general-classroom placement on support rather than treating placement alone as sufficient. U.S. statutory text is not copyrightable.

title: IDEA Sec. 1414(d)(3)(B)(i) - Consideration of special factors
provider: U.S. Department of Education, IDEA statute site (Office of Special Education Programs)
notes: Federal statutory text: when a child's behavior impedes that child's learning or the learning of others, the IEP team must consider the use of positive behavioral interventions and supports and other strategies to address the behavior. Used to show where operant-derived practice is embedded in U.S. law. U.S. statutory text is not copyrightable.

title: 20 U.S.C. 1418(d) - Disproportionality
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA statute site)
notes: Statutory text requiring States to determine whether significant disproportionality based on race and ethnicity is occurring in identification (including identification by particular impairment), placement in particular educational settings, and the incidence, duration, and type of disciplinary actions including suspensions and expulsions; and requiring policy review and revision, reservation of early intervening services funds, and public reporting when it is found. Used to establish that IDEA itself, not only outside critics, treats racial disproportionality as a compliance problem.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.111 - Child find
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the affirmative duty to identify, locate, and evaluate all children with disabilities residing in the State, including homeless children, wards of the State, and children in private schools, regardless of severity of disability; and for (c), which extends child find to children suspected of having a disability even though they are advancing from grade to grade, and to highly mobile children including migrant children.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.114 - LRE requirements
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the LRE presumption at (a)(2)(i) - to the maximum extent appropriate, children with disabilities are educated with children who are nondisabled - and for (a)(2)(ii), permitting special classes, separate schooling, or other removal only if the nature or severity of the disability is such that education in regular classes with supplementary aids and services cannot be achieved satisfactorily.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.115 - Continuum of alternative placements
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the requirement that each public agency ensure a continuum of alternative placements is available - instruction in regular classes, special classes, special schools, home instruction, and instruction in hospitals and institutions - and that supplementary services such as a resource room or itinerant instruction be available in conjunction with regular class placement. Supports the lesson's treatment of LRE as a continuum rather than a binary.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.116 - Placements
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the requirements that the placement decision be made by a group including the parents, be determined at least annually, be based on the child's IEP, be as close as possible to the child's home, that the child be educated in the school he or she would attend if nondisabled unless the IEP requires otherwise, and that a child not be removed from age-appropriate regular classrooms solely because of needed modifications in the general education curriculum. Supplies the ordering rule that services are decided before placement.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.226 - Early intervening services
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the 15 percent cap on Part B funds an LEA may use for early intervening services, and for the population served: students in kindergarten through grade 12, with particular emphasis on kindergarten through grade three, who are not currently identified as needing special education or related services but who need additional academic and behavioral support to succeed in a general education environment. Supplies the percentage behind the 'maximum amount of funds' reservation triggered by significant disproportionality.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.301 - Initial evaluations
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the rule that either a parent or a public agency may initiate a request for an initial evaluation, for the parental consent requirement cross-referenced to 300.300, and for the 60-day timeline in (c)(1) running from receipt of parental consent, subject to a State-established timeframe where one exists.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.304 - Evaluation procedures
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for (b)(1) requiring a variety of assessment tools and strategies; (b)(2) prohibiting any single measure or assessment as the sole criterion for determining disability; (c)(1) requiring that materials not be discriminatory on a racial or cultural basis and be administered in the child's native language or other mode of communication; (c)(4) requiring assessment in all areas related to the suspected disability; and (c)(6) requiring the evaluation to be sufficiently comprehensive to identify all special education and related services needs whether or not commonly linked to the disability category.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.306 - Determination of eligibility
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for (a)(1), under which a group of qualified professionals and the parent of the child determine eligibility, and for the special rule at (b)(1) barring a disability determination where the determinant factor is lack of appropriate instruction in reading including the essential components of reading instruction, lack of appropriate instruction in math, or limited English proficiency. This is the authority for the lesson's point that instructional failure and language acquisition must be ruled out before eligibility is found.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.320 - Definition of individualized education program
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the required contents of an IEP at (a)(1)-(a)(7): present levels of academic achievement and functional performance including the effect of the disability on involvement and progress in the general education curriculum; measurable annual academic and functional goals; how and when progress will be measured and reported; special education, related services, supplementary aids and services based on peer-reviewed research to the extent practicable, and program modifications or supports for school personnel; an explanation of the extent, if any, to which the child will not participate with nondisabled children; accommodations for State and districtwide assessments; and projected start date, frequency, location, and duration. Also used for (b), transition services beginning not later than the first IEP in effect when the child turns 16, or younger if the Team determines it appropriate.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.321 - IEP Team
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for required IEP Team membership at (a): the parents; not less than one regular education teacher of the child if the child is or may be participating in the regular education environment; not less than one special education teacher or provider; a representative of the public agency qualified to provide or supervise specially designed instruction and knowledgeable about the general education curriculum and agency resources; an individual who can interpret the instructional implications of evaluation results; other individuals with knowledge or special expertise at the discretion of the parent or agency; and, whenever appropriate, the child. Supports the lesson's treatment of parent participation as a structural requirement rather than a courtesy.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.39 - Special education
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the definition of special education as specially designed instruction, at no cost to parents, to meet the unique needs of a child with a disability, delivered in classrooms, homes, hospitals, institutions and other settings; and for (b)(3), specially designed instruction as adapting the content, methodology, or delivery of instruction to address needs resulting from the disability and to ensure access to the general curriculum. This is the authority for the lesson's claim that special education is a service rather than a place.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.504 - Procedural safeguards notice
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for when the safeguards notice must be given (generally once a school year, plus at initial referral or parent-requested evaluation, on receipt of the first State or due process complaint in a school year, in accordance with the discipline procedures, and on parent request) and for the full list of safeguards the notice must explain, including independent educational evaluations, prior written notice, parental consent, access to education records, State and due process complaint procedures, mediation, placement during pendency, unilateral private placement, hearings, State-level appeals, civil actions, and attorneys' fees.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.506 - Mediation
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the requirements that mediation be available for any matter under Part B, be voluntary on the part of the parties, not be used to deny or delay a parent's right to a due process hearing or any other right, and be conducted by a qualified and impartial mediator trained in effective mediation techniques.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.507 - Filing a due process complaint
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for who may file (a parent or a public agency), the subject matter (identification, evaluation, or educational placement of a child with a disability, or the provision of FAPE), and the two-year limitation running from when the party knew or should have known about the alleged action, subject to exceptions.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.518 - Child's status during proceedings
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the stay-put rule: during the pendency of any administrative or judicial proceeding regarding a due process complaint, unless the agency and parents agree otherwise, the child must remain in his or her current educational placement. Used in the lesson to show that procedural safeguards have substantive consequences during a dispute.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.646 - Disproportionality
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the State duty to determine significant disproportionality based on race and ethnicity with respect to identification (overall and by particular impairment), placement in particular educational settings, and the incidence, duration, and type of disciplinary removals including suspensions and expulsions; and for the consequences - annual review and revision of policies, practices, and procedures, reservation of the maximum early intervening services funds for comprehensive coordinated early intervening services, and public reporting. Also used for the rule that an LEA may not limit comprehensive coordinated early intervening services to children with disabilities and may serve children from age 3 through grade 12.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.647 - Determining significant disproportionality
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: Used for the standard methodology States must apply: a risk ratio comparing the risk of an outcome for one racial or ethnic group in an LEA against the risk for all other groups in that LEA, or an alternate risk ratio using the State comparison group when LEA comparison data are insufficient; the seven racial and ethnic groups analyzed; the outcome categories analyzed for identification, placement, and discipline; and each State's obligation to set a reasonable risk ratio threshold, minimum cell size, and minimum n-size.

title: 34 C.F.R. 300.8 - Child with a disability
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA regulations site)
notes: The eligibility definition. Used for the two-part test in (a)(1) - evaluated as having one of the listed conditions 'and who, by reason thereof, needs special education and related services'; for (a)(2), under which a child needing only a related service is not a child with a disability unless that service is considered special education under State standards; for the 13 enumerated categories in (c) and their subsection letters; for the 'adversely affects educational performance' language carried in the individual category definitions; and for the optional developmental delay category in (b) for children aged three through nine. This is the primary authority for the lesson's central point that a medical diagnosis alone does not establish IDEA eligibility.

title: 34 C.F.R. 303.344 - Content of an IFSP
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (IDEA Part C regulations site)
notes: Used for the contents of the Individualized Family Service Plan under Part C: present levels of physical, cognitive, communication, social or emotional, and adaptive development; a statement of the family's resources, priorities, and concerns related to enhancing the development of the child; measurable results or outcomes for child and family; early intervention services based on peer-reviewed research to the extent practicable with length, duration, frequency, intensity, and method of delivery; the natural environments statement or justification; a named service coordinator; and steps supporting transition out of Part C. Supplies the concrete basis for the lesson's IFSP-versus-IEP contrast.

title: John Dewey (1859-1952)
provider: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
notes: Peer-reviewed philosophy reference. Supports Dewey's instrumentalism, the University of Chicago laboratory school (1896-1904), The School and Society (1899), Democracy and Education (1916), and his view of the school as continuous with civil society. All rights reserved; facts synthesized, no wording reused.

title: Teaching Secondary Students to Write Effectively (WWC Practice Guide, November 2016; revised December 2019)
provider: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Federal practice guide (Graham et al.) used for Recommendation 1, explicitly teaching appropriate writing strategies using a Model-Practice-Reflect instructional cycle, rated strong evidence. Used as the strongest official evidence that a modeling-based instructional cycle works in a real subject area. Reuse terms not separately verified; recorded as reference only.

title: Accommodations: Instructional and Testing Supports for Students with Disabilities (IRIS Module, Page 1)
provider: The IRIS Center, Peabody College, Vanderbilt University (U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs, Grant #H325E220001)
license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
notes: Used for the definition of accommodations as adaptations to educational environments and practices that change how students access learning rather than what they learn, for the explicit statement that accommodations do not alter learning expectations or reduce task requirements, and for the four accommodation categories (presentation, response, setting, timing and scheduling). The licence forbids derivative works, so no IRIS wording is adapted; the categories are named as facts and all surrounding prose is original.

title: Behavioral Form and Function (Functional Behavioral Assessment: Elementary, Page 1)
provider: The IRIS Center, Peabody College, Vanderbilt University, supported by a cooperative agreement with the U.S. Department of Education, Office of Special Education Programs (Grant H325E220001)
license: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International (stated on the page)
notes: OSEP-funded teacher-preparation module page used for the four functions of behavior as they are taught to educators - attention, items or activities, escape, and automatic or sensory - and for the framing that each function corresponds to a fundamental need and that a behavior that pays off in reinforcement becomes more likely to recur. The CC BY-NC-ND licence bars derivative use, so the page was used for facts only and nothing was adapted.

title: Lobbying (charities and nonprofits)
provider: Internal Revenue Service, U.S. Department of the Treasury

notes: Used for the decision date (May 18, 1896), citation 163 U.S. 537, the 1890 Louisiana Separate Car Act, the 7-1 vote with Harlan dissenting, and the 'separate but equal' doctrine.

title: Proactive Policing: Effects on Crime and Communities (2018), Chapter 7, Conclusions 7-1 and 7-2
provider: Committee on Proactive Policing, Committee on Law and Justice, National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine; The National Academies Press
notes: Consensus study report, David Weisburd and Malay K. Majmundar, editors; front matter states Copyright 2018 by the National Academy of Sciences, all rights reserved. Chapter 7 read in full through the National Academies online reader at https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/24928/chapter/9. Used for Conclusion 7-1 (large racial disparities are likely where police target high-risk people or places), Conclusion 7-2 (existing evidence does not conclusively establish whether or how much those disparities indicate statistical prediction, racial animus, implicit bias, or other causes), the chapter's discussion of the benchmark problem, and its observation that clear agency guidelines can reduce biased behavior by reducing discretion. No prose reproduced.

title: How People Learn II: Learners, Contexts, and Cultures, Chapter 4: Processes That Support Learning
provider: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine; The National Academies Press
notes: Consensus study report used for the reconstructive character of memory (learning and memory systems produce knowledge without storing copies of it), for the role of prior knowledge and prior experience in shaping mental representations, for the importance of the retrieval cues available in the learner's environment, and for the association between working memory capacity and academic achievement in mathematics and reading.

title: Proactive Policing: Effects on Crime and Communities
provider: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Committee on Law and Justice (National Academies Press, 2018)
notes: Read the report Summary and Chapter 6 online (DOI 10.17226/24928). Source for the four elements of procedural justice as the committee sets them out (voice, neutrality, respect, trustworthiness, drawn from Tyler's work), for Conclusion 6-4 that perceptions of procedurally just treatment are strongly associated with judgements of legitimacy and cooperation but that the evidence base is insufficient to conclude the relationship is causal, and for Conclusion 4-11 that the evidence base on procedural justice policing and crime is very small and supports no conclusion either way. Also the source for the committee's caution that insufficient evidence is not evidence of absence. Copyright National Academy of Sciences; no wording reproduced.

title: NASW Code of Ethics (2021 revision), including Ethical Responsibilities to Clients
provider: National Association of Social Workers
notes: Primary source for the six core values, the Code's six stated purposes, the aspirational-versus-enforceable distinction, the statement that the Code does not prescribe conduct for all situations, the statement that violating a standard does not automatically imply legal liability, the six sections of ethical standards, and standards 1.01-1.04 (commitment to clients, self-determination and the serious/foreseeable/imminent risk limit, informed consent and capacity, competence). Copyrighted; described in original wording only, no text reproduced.

title: Person-in-Environment System Manual, 2nd Edition (sample chapters: Structure of the PIE System; How to Use PIE in Practice)
provider: NASW Press - James M. Karls and Maura E. O'Keefe
notes: Publisher-posted sample chapters of the PIE System manual (2nd ed., NASW Press, 2008, ISBN 978-0-87101-379-8; publisher page https://naswpress.org/product/person-in-environment-system-manual/ confirms authors, edition and year, and describes PIE as an alternative to disease and moral models). Text extracted and read. Confirms the four factors (I Social Functioning / Social Role and Relationship Problems; II Environmental Problems; III Mental Health; IV Physical Health), that Factors I and II are the core social work description while III and IV borrow other professions' classifications, the six Factor II system types, the strengths component, and the manual's explicit statement that PIE is not an interview guide. Copyrighted; no wording reproduced.

title: NASW Standards for Social Work Case Management (2013)
provider: National Association of Social Workers
notes: Primary source for the profession's definition of case management (planning, seeking, advocating for, and monitoring services across organizations to limit fragmentation), the twelve standards and their titles, Standard 8 on interdisciplinary and interorganizational collaboration, Standard 10 on record keeping (clinical continuity, reimbursement and utilization review, support in the event of legal review, and the listed record elements), Standard 11 on workload sustainability (caseload versus workload; the variables that make a caseload number uninterpretable on its own; organizational responsibility), and the note that terminology for the people served varies by setting and funder. Copyright (c) 2013 NASW, all rights reserved; read via local PDF text extraction and restated in original wording.

title: Condition of Education: Public School Revenue Sources
provider: National Center for Education Statistics, Institute of Education Sciences
notes: Used for school year 2020-21 public school revenues: 11 percent federal, 46 percent state, 44 percent local.

title: Condition of Education: Students With Disabilities (last updated May 2024)
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Statistics
notes: Checked live on 2026-08-18; the most recent data year on the indicator is school year 2022-23 and the page is marked last updated May 2024, so the lesson dates the figures rather than presenting them as current-year. Used for 7.5 million students ages 3-21 served under IDEA in 2022-23, equal to 15 percent of all public school students; for the category distribution (specific learning disabilities 32 percent, speech or language impairments 19 percent, other health impairments 15 percent, autism 13 percent, developmental delay 7 percent, intellectual disability 6 percent, emotional disturbance 4 percent); and for the percentage of public school students served by race and ethnicity (American Indian/Alaska Native 19, Black 17, White 15, Hispanic 14, Pacific Islander 12, Asian 8). Figures and their attribution were taken; the page's prose was not adapted.

title: Digest of Education Statistics, Table 219.10: High school graduates and total graduates as a ratio of 17-year-old population
provider: National Center for Education Statistics, Institute of Education Sciences
notes: Used for the graduate-to-17-year-old ratios: 2.0 percent (1869-70), 3.5 percent (1889-90), 6.4 percent (1899-1900), 16.8 percent (1919-20), 50.8 percent (1939-40), 69.5 percent (1959-60), 87.9 percent (2021-22).

title: Fast Facts: Inclusion of Students With Disabilities (indicator 59)
provider: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Statistics
notes: Used for fall 2022 placement data: 95 percent of students ages 5-21 served under IDEA were enrolled in regular schools, 2 percent in separate schools for students with disabilities, 2 percent parentally placed in private schools, and 1 percent homebound, hospitalized, or in other facilities; 67 percent of those in regular schools spent 80 percent or more of their time in general classes, up from 61 percent in fall 2012; and the spread across categories, from 89 percent for speech or language impairments to 21 percent for intellectual disabilities. These figures give the lesson's LRE section an empirical anchor showing that the continuum is genuinely used and used unevenly.

title: NAEP Technical Documentation: Backreading
provider: National Center for Education Statistics, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Supports the definition of backreading as a supervisor reviewing already-scored responses to check that the scoring guide is being applied correctly, the target of backreading at least five percent of all scorer work on a daily basis, and the practice of resuming group training when backreading reveals errors common to several scorers.

title: NAEP Technical Documentation: Scoring Monitoring
provider: National Center for Education Statistics, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Supports the description of ongoing scorer monitoring in a large operational programme: trainers responsible for keeping team interrater agreement high, calibration sets used to stop teams drifting from the scoring standard, within-year interrater agreement checks, and trend scoring used to compare agreement across years.

title: National Standards of Practice for Interpreters in Health Care
provider: National Council on Interpreting in Health Care
notes: September 2005; 32 standards under nine headings. Supports the accuracy standards (render all messages completely without adding, omitting, or substituting; replicate register, style, and tone; advise parties that everything will be interpreted; manage flow; correct errors; maintain transparency), the respect standards (promote direct communication among parties), and the role-boundary standards (limit professional activity to interpreting; never advise, but redirect).

title: Mental Health Professionals' Duty to Warn (brief and fifty-state chart, updated March 16, 2022)
provider: National Conference of State Legislatures
notes: Source for most states either requiring or permitting mental health professionals to disclose information about patients who may become violent, for Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1976) triggering duty-to-warn and duty-to-protect laws in almost every state, and for the fifty-state chart classifying jurisdictions as mandatory, permissive, or no duty with differing triggers, covered professions, and discharging actions. Used qualitatively; no count published in the lesson.

title: Restoration of Voting Rights for Felons (brief and fifty-state tables, updated May 20, 2026)
provider: National Conference of State Legislatures
notes: Source of the four-category state breakdown of felony disenfranchisement and restoration, with per-state constitutional and statutory citations. No reuse license stated; facts used, wording not reproduced.

title: Center for Universal Design
provider: College of Design, North Carolina State University
notes: Used for Ronald Mace as founder, the center's establishment in 1989 as the Center for Accessible Housing under a National Institute on Disability and Rehabilitation Research grant, the definition of universal design as the design of products and environments to be usable by all people to the greatest extent possible without the need for adaptation or specialized design, the seven Principles of Universal Design (equitable use, flexibility in use, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, size and space for approach and use) dated Version 2.0, 4/1/97, and the note that the center is currently inactive due to funding. title: Rubric Best Practices, Examples, and Templates
provider: DELTA (Digital Education and Learning Technology Applications), NC State University

title: National Inventory of Collateral Consequences of Conviction (NICCC)
provider: Council of State Governments Justice Center, funded in part by the Bureau of Justice Assistance, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: The authoritative catalogue of U.S. collateral consequences, covering all 50 states, the federal system, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, searchable by consequence type, offense type, whether the consequence is mandatory or discretionary, and duration. No reuse license stated; used for scope and structure only, and its own disclaimer states the site is educational and not legal advice.

title: Words Matter: Preferred Language for Talking About Addiction
provider: National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health
notes: Supports the lesson's language-choice method: person-first phrasing separates the person from the condition, stigmatizing terms reduce willingness to seek help and lower a person's sense of hope and self-efficacy, and federal guidance recommends describing condition or behavior rather than labeling people. Used as reference only; wording not reproduced.

title: Research on Body-Worn Cameras and Law Enforcement
provider: National Institute of Justice, Office of Justice Programs, U.S. Department of Justice
notes: Page states Date Published January 7, 2022 and Date Modified January 22, 2023; retrieved with a browser user agent because the plain fetcher was served a partial page. Used for NIJ's characterization of the evidence as mixed, the review of 70 studies finding no consistent or no statistically significant effects, the CrimeSolutions No Effects practice rating covering use of force, assaults on officers, officer-initiated calls for service, arrests, traffic stops and tickets, and field interviews, and the range of individual program ratings from Effective (Boston) through Promising to No Effects (Washington, D.C.). U.S. government work; paraphrased only.

title: Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study (ABCD Study)
provider: National Institute of Mental Health, U.S. National Institutes of Health
notes: Federal agency page used to corroborate the ABCD Study's scale and design from a government source: nearly 12,000 youth at 21 U.S. research sites followed from ages 9 and 10 into early adulthood, with brain imaging alongside measures of screen time, sleep, activities, family, and substance exposure, and with academic achievement, cognitive skills, and mental health among the tracked outcomes. No reuse statement appears on the page, so it is recorded reference only.

title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) - health topic page
provider: National Institute of Mental Health, U.S. National Institutes of Health
notes: Verified that many people who live through a dangerous event experience some symptoms initially but most do not develop PTSD, that most people recover from those initial symptoms, and that a PTSD diagnosis turns on symptoms lasting an extended period and interfering with daily life. Corroborates the VA prevalence framing and supports the statement that diagnosis rests on clinical criteria rather than on any test.

title: The Teen Brain: 7 Things to Know
provider: National Institute of Mental Health, U.S. National Institutes of Health
license: U.S. public domain (the page states the information is in the public domain and may be reused or copied without permission, excluding images)
notes: Federal health agency publication. Used for the statements that adolescence is an important period for brain development; that the prefrontal cortex, responsible for planning, prioritizing, and decision making, is one of the last parts to mature and that the brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late twenties; that the combination of a peer-oriented social brain and continuing prefrontal development may push teens toward risk-taking because social benefits outweigh possible consequences; that the teen brain is ready to learn and adapt; and that it is resilient. Also used to show that the same federal source that names the mid-to-late twenties also emphasizes adolescent learning capacity, which is the part the popular slogan drops.

title: The Assumption of a Reliable Instrument and Other Pitfalls to Avoid When Considering the Reliability of Data (Frontiers in Psychology, 2012)
provider: Kim Nimon, Linda Reichwein Zientek and Robin K. Henson; PubMed Central (PMC3324779)
license: Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial License (as stated on the article)
notes: Used for the claim that reliability is a property of scores rather than of instruments and that citing a manual's coefficient as though it described one's own sample is an error, and for the caution that the attenuation story holds under classical assumptions: when error scores correlate with true scores or with one another, an observed correlation can exceed its true-score counterpart. The lesson therefore states the attenuation ceiling as a consequence of the classical model rather than as a universal law.

title: Gagne's Nine Events of Instruction (Instructional Guide for University Faculty and Teaching Assistants)
provider: Center for Innovative Teaching and Learning, Northern Illinois University
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
notes: University teaching-center guide used for the names and order of Gagne's nine events, and for the underlying citations to Gagne, Briggs and Wager (1992) and Gagne (1985). Licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the NonCommercial term has not been cleared for this project, so the record is REFERENCE_ONLY and only the event names - which originate with Gagne, not with NIU - are carried through.

title: Concerted activity (Rights We Protect)
provider: National Labor Relations Board
notes: Read for the agency's description of protected concerted activity: employees acting together on work-related issues such as discussing wages or working conditions, circulating a petition about hours, or refusing to work in unsafe conditions; the protection of an individual acting on the authority of other employees, bringing group complaints, inducing group action, or preparing for group action; and the statement that an employer may not discharge, discipline, threaten, or coercively question employees for such activity. The page did not state the statutory exclusions, which were verified separately against 29 U.S.C. 152.

title: Conditioning and Learning (Noba Textbook Series: Psychology)
provider: Mark E. Bouton / Noba Project, DEF Publishers
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (as stated on the module page)
notes: Research-authored open module used for classical vs operant definitions, Thorndike's law of effect, stimulus control / discriminative stimuli, extinction as inhibition rather than erasure (spontaneous recovery, renewal), and the reinforcer-devaluation finding that learners encode outcome expectancies. NonCommercial-ShareAlike terms were not cleared for this project, so the module was used as reference only and no wording was adapted.

title: Forgetting and Amnesia
provider: Nicole Dudukovic and Brice Kuhl / Noba Project, DEF Publishers
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (as stated on the module page)
notes: Tier B open textbook. Supports the taxonomy of causes of forgetting, the criticism of decay theory (disuse does not guarantee forgetting; consolidation-disruption accounts), the proactive/retroactive interference definitions, and cue-dependent retrieval failure. Facts only; no wording reproduced.

title: Memory (Encoding, Storage, Retrieval) (Noba Textbook Series: Psychology)
provider: Kathleen B. McDermott and Henry L. Roediger III / Noba Project, DEF Publishers
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (as stated on the module page)
notes: Research-authored open module used for the encoding-storage-retrieval framing, retrieval cues, the encoding specificity principle, cue overload, and the point that retrieval itself alters memory. NonCommercial and ShareAlike terms were not cleared for this project, so it was used as reference only and no wording was adapted.

title: Ivan Pavlov - Biographical, The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1904
provider: The Nobel Foundation / NobelPrize.org
notes: Confirms Pavlov's 1904 prize was awarded for work on the physiology of digestion, that his study of 'psychic secretion' led him to conditioned (temporary) reflexes, and that he worked on the formation of conditioned reflexes until his death in 1936. Facts synthesized; wording not reused.

title: Ethical Standards for Human Services Professionals (adopted 2024)
provider: National Organization for Human Services
notes: Source for the human services profession having its own code organized by responsibility domains (public and society, clients, employers, colleagues, students, profession, self), Standard 2 informed consent including clients unable to consent and mandated services, Standard 4 safety-based disclosure in accordance with state and federal law, Standard 12 duty to be informed about relevant law, Standard 24 managing employer-versus-client conflicts, Standard 26 scope of practice, and Standard 28 consultation and supervision in dilemmas. Reproduction permitted only in entirety for non-commercial use; treated as reference only.

title: Relationship between School Suspension and Student Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis (School Psychology Review, 44(2), 224-240; ERIC EJ1141532)
provider: Amity L. Noltemeyer, Rose Marie Ward and Caven Mcloughlin; School Psychology Review, via ERIC
notes: Peer-reviewed catalogue record retrieved through the ERIC API. Used for the meta-analysis scope (53 cases from 34 studies, peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed, 1986-2012), for the significant inverse relationship between suspension and achievement and the significant positive relationship between suspension and dropout, and for the finding that suspension type and study or participant characteristics moderated those relationships. The full text was not retrievable, so no effect-size magnitudes are cited and the lesson describes the findings as associations.

title: Hull-House
provider: National Park Service, U.S. Department of the Interior
notes: Federal historical reference. Confirms Hull-House was established in Chicago in 1889 by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr as the first settlement house in the United States, that it provided direct services (legal aid, employment office, childcare, training), and that residents pursued neighbourhood and structural reform including protective labour laws and housing and sanitation problems. Used for the settlement-house half of PIE's intellectual inheritance.

title: Setting the Precedent: Mendez, et al. v. Westminster School District of Orange County, et al.
provider: U.S. National Park Service
notes: Used for Judge Paul J. McCormick's February 1946 district court ruling, the Ninth Circuit affirmance, the subsequent California repeal of school segregation statutes signed by Governor Earl Warren, and the NAACP brief by Carter, Marshall, and Miller. The article's dating of the appellate decision conflicts with the reporter year and is logged under conflictingEvidence.

title: Minority Students in Special and Gifted Education (2002)
provider: Committee on Minority Representation in Special Education, National Research Council of the National Academies; National Academies Press
notes: Consensus study report of a National Research Council committee convened at the request of the Office for Civil Rights. Used for the existence and framing of the disproportionate-representation problem and for the range of contributors the committee examined - early biological and environmental influences, inequities in preschool and K-12 opportunity, and possible bias in the referral and assessment system - and for the point that racial and ethnic disproportion in gifted and talented programs generally runs in the opposite direction. Cited to establish that this is a long-standing, seriously studied question, not to settle it. Copyrighted; no wording reproduced.

title: How People Learn: Brain, Mind, Experience, and School - Expanded Edition
provider: National Research Council, Committee on Developments in the Science of Learning; National Academies Press (2000)
notes: National Academies consensus synthesis. Used for the first key finding - that students arrive with preconceptions about how the world works and that unengaged initial understandings leave them unable to grasp new concepts or liable to revert after a test - and for the accompanying implication that teachers must draw out and work with existing understandings. Also used for the point that misconceptions are treated as errors to be addressed, not as equally valid alternatives. Readable free online but under National Academy of Sciences copyright; no wording reproduced.

title: New York Education Law Section 6513 - Unauthorized use of a professional title a crime
provider: New York State Legislature (via NY Senate legislation portal)
notes: General title-protection provision covering all professions regulated under Title VIII of the Education Law, including social work: unauthorized use of a regulated professional title is a class A misdemeanor. Added after a verification pass showed that section 7706 alone restricts only other enumerated licensed professionals, not the public at large, so the lesson's title-protection statement was corrected to rest on this section. Statute text summarized, not quoted at length.

title: New York Education Law Section 7701 - Definition of practice of licensed master social work and licensed clinical social work
provider: New York State Legislature (via NY Senate legislation portal)
notes: Documented single-state example showing that a state can define legally distinct master's-level and clinical scopes, with diagnosis, psychotherapy, and treatment planning reserved to the clinical license. Statutes are edicts of government and not copyrightable; the host site is behind a bot challenge, so the text was read through a rendering fetch rather than bulk retrieval. Provisions summarized, not quoted at length.

title: New York Education Law Section 7706 - Exempt persons
provider: New York State Legislature (via NY Senate legislation portal)
notes: Documented single-state example of title protection plus scope exemptions: the titles licensed clinical social worker and licensed master social worker are reserved to persons licensed under the article, while unlicensed staff may perform screening, assessment, referral, non-clinical service planning, case management, and peer services, with diagnosis and psychotherapy restricted. Used to ground the social work / human services scope distinction in actual law and explicitly labelled in the lesson as one state's rules.

title: New York Penal Law section 35.15 - Justification; use of physical force in defense of a person
provider: New York State Senate
notes: Supports the reasonable-belief and imminence language, and the duty-to-retreat rule in subdivision 2(a) with its exceptions, including the actor's own dwelling when not the initial aggressor and officers acting under section 35.30. Used as the contrasting jurisdiction to Florida.

title: New York Penal Law 10.00 - Definitions of terms of general use in this chapter
provider: New York State Senate (official legislation site)
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Supports the New York definitions of offense, violation, misdemeanor, felony, and crime, including the fifteen-day ceiling on a violation and the one-year felony line.

title: New York Penal Law 55.05 - Classifications of felonies and misdemeanors
provider: New York State Senate (official legislation site)
license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Supports the New York letter classes: five felony categories (A-I and A-II within Class A, plus B, C, D, E) and three misdemeanor categories (A, B, unclassified).

title: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) Teams Guidelines (2025)
provider: New York State Office of Mental Health
notes: Read in full via local PDF text extraction. Supports the structural specification of ACT: multidisciplinary team, in vivo services, a 10:1 caseload ratio, shared caseload with team-level responsibility, services for as long as needed, flexible delivery via daily team meetings, and availability 24 hours a day 7 days a week; admission indicators including two or more psychiatric inpatient admissions in 12 months or one hospitalization of 60 days or more; assessment as an ongoing process reviewed at least every six months and reconsidered after significant events; daily team meeting review of hospitalizations, incarcerations, risk and emerging needs; transition and discharge planning; documentation and progress-note requirements tied to reimbursement; and required staff competence in person-centered language and cultural humility. No reuse licence stated; described in original wording.

title: Topic Brief 4: The Zone of Proximal Development - An Affirmative Perspective in Teaching ELLs and MLs
provider: New York State Education Department, Office of Bilingual Education and World Languages; brief authored by Elsa Billings and Aida Walqui (WestEd)
notes: State education agency guidance. Used to confirm the standard English rendering of Vygotsky's definition of the zone of proximal development - the distance between the actual developmental level shown in independent problem solving and the level of potential development shown under adult guidance or in collaboration with more capable peers - and for the practical point that assistance in the zone can come from adults, more capable peers, and equal peers. Reuse terms are not stated on the page, so it is recorded reference only.

title: Writing Performance Objectives
provider: New York State Education Department, Adult Career and Continuing Education Services / Bureau of Proprietary School Supervision

Page carries a NYSED copyright notice; no wording reproduced.

provider: Open Oregon Educational Resources (chapter by Aikia Fricke and Ferris State University Department of Social Work)

Supports the standard descriptions of the eco-map as a diagram of an individual's social and personal relationships with their environment, credited to Ann Hartman in the mid-1970s, and of Bronfenbrenner's five levels as they are taught in human services. No prose adapted; used to verify the conventional teaching.

title: International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, Article 13
provider: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights
notes: Official OHCHR PDF of the Covenant (HTTP 200 on 2026-08-18; the OHCHR HTML instrument page returns 403 to fetchers). Article 13 supplies the treaty-level obligations that turn the declaratory right into binding duties, including free compulsory primary education, progressive introduction of free secondary and higher education, and fundamental education for those who did not complete primary schooling.

title: Universal Design for Learning in Pre-K to Grade 12 Classrooms: A Systematic Review of Research (Exceptionality, 25(2), 116-138)
provider: Min Wook Ok, Kavita Rao, Brian R. Bryant, Dennis McDougall; Education Resources Information Center (ERIC EJ1135477), IES, U.S. Department of Education
notes: ERIC record read for the review's scope (13 qualifying studies of UDL-based instruction in pre-K to grade 12), its finding that UDL-based instruction has potential to increase engagement and access to the general education curriculum, and - critically for this lesson's honest evidence statement - that efficacy varied considerably within and across studies with effect sizes from small to large, and that authors were inconsistent in reporting the connection between specific UDL guidelines and intervention components. Article full text is paywalled; only the ERIC record was used, and no wording reproduced.

title: The effectiveness of community engagement in public health interventions for disadvantaged groups: a meta-analysis
provider: O'Mara-Eves A, Brunton G, Oliver S, Kavanagh J, Jamal F, Thomas J; BMC Public Health 15:129
license: CC BY 4.0

No wording reused.

Dated in the lesson because executive guidance is revisable; no wording reproduced.

title: A paradigm shift: relationships in trauma-informed mental health services (BJPsych Advances 24(5), 319-333)
provider: Sweeney A, Filson B, Kennedy A, Collinson L, Gillard S; Royal College of Psychiatrists / Cambridge University Press

title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later (Educational Psychology Review, 31(2), 261-292)
provider: John Sweller, Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer, Fred Paas; ERIC record EJ1217401
notes: Used for the architectural premise of cognitive load theory - that novel information is first processed by a working memory limited in capacity and duration and then stored in an effectively unlimited long-term memory for later use - and for the point that instructional design long proceeded without reference to those structures. Abstract-level verification only; no wording reproduced.

title: Why Minimally Guided Teaching Techniques Do Not Work: A Reply to Commentaries
provider: Sweller, J., Kirschner, P. A., & Clark, R. E.; Educational Psychologist 42(2), 115-121 (2007); ERIC EJ772219
notes: Abstract read through the ERIC API; bibliographic details confirmed through Crossref (DOI 10.1080/00461520701263426). Used to show that the exchange did not end in agreement: the original authors reasserted randomized controlled comparisons that alter one variable at a time and rejected reducing the presentation of relevant information in favor of teaching learners how to find information.

title: History of Education in the United States: Seminal Works, Critical Analyses, Landmark Studies and Foundational Texts
provider: Syracuse University Libraries
notes: Used to establish that the interpretive disagreement is real and to identify the works that define it: Cremin's Transformation of the School (1961), Michael B. Katz's Irony of Early School Reform, Bowles and Gintis's Schooling in Capitalist America, Kaestle's Pillars of the Republic (1983), Tyack's One Best System (1974), and Anderson's Education of Blacks in the South, 1860-1935. The lesson cites the debate, not any book's specific arguments beyond what this guide characterizes.

title: Maxine Greene, TC's Great Philosopher, Dies at 96
provider: Teachers College, Columbia University
notes: Institutional memorial supporting Greene's dates (1917-2014), her position at Teachers College from 1965, her existentialist and phenomenological sources (Sartre, Beauvoir, Merleau-Ponty), and her concepts of wide-awakeness, imagination, freedom and aesthetic education.

title: Cultural Humility Versus Cultural Competence: A Critical Distinction in Defining Physician Training Outcomes in Multicultural Education (Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, 9(2), 117-125)
provider: Melanie Tervalon and Jann Murray-Garcia; Johns Hopkins University Press. Full text read from the scanned copy of the published article posted by the first author on her professional site; bibliographic record and abstract independently confirmed against the MEDLINE record served by Europe PMC (PMID 10073197, DOI 10.1353/hpu.2010.0233).
notes: The originating source for the concept. Read page by page (pp. 117-125). Supports: the three commitments as the authors stated them; the objection to competence understood as an easily demonstrable mastery of a finite body of knowledge evidenced by comparative quantitative assessment; the nurse anecdote in which self-proclaimed cultural expertise led to a patient's postoperative pain being dismissed; the authors' explicit statement that they are in no way discounting the value of knowing as much as possible about the health care practices of the communities served; the coining example; the physician relinquishing the role of expert and becoming the student of the patient; patient-focused interviewing described as a less controlling, less authoritative style; Ridley's example of a patient's conjoint membership in eight cultural roles and the intersection of race, ethnicity, religion and class; the Institutional consistency section, including the question of whether an institution that teaches against using children or family members as translators actually provides an accessible alternative; and the authors' own statement that measurement of cultural competence was not a well-developed area of research. No wording is reproduced; all prose in the lesson is original.

title: What would help low-income families? Results from a North American survey of 2-1-1 helpline professionals
provider: Thompson T, Roux AM, Kohl PL, Boyum S, Kreuter MW; Journal of Child Health Care 22(4):670-683; author manuscript on PubMed Central
notes: Abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 29788775). Supports the supporting claim that information-and-referral staff themselves judge community resources inadequate for some need categories: 471 information and referral specialists, resource managers and call center directors from 44 states, Puerto Rico and Canada were surveyed, and across all child care dimensions asked about, more than half rated community resources inadequate. Used as corroboration of the scarcity theme only; the survey's ranking of which needs matter most is not used.

title: The Standard Error of Measurement Is a More Appropriate Measure of Quality for Postgraduate Medical Assessments Than Is Reliability: An Analysis of MRCP(UK) Examinations (BMC Medical Education, 10:40)
provider: Jennifer Tighe, I. C. McManus, Nicholas G. Dewhurst, Liliana Chis and John Mucklow; PubMed Central (PMC2893515)
license: Creative Commons Attribution License 2.0
notes: Used for the classical relationship between the standard error of measurement, the score standard deviation and the reliability coefficient; for the range-restriction demonstration in which restricting the MRCP(UK) sample to already-passing candidates dropped reliability from about .90 to about .70 while the standard error of measurement was essentially unchanged; and for the framing that reliability is a joint property of an assessment and the candidates who happen to take it while the standard error behaves more like a property of the measuring instrument. The lesson's own worked example uses different, original numbers. Licence permits reuse with attribution, but no prose was reproduced.

title: The Role of Wait Time in Higher Cognitive Level Learning (Review of Educational Research, 57(1), 69-95)
provider: Kenneth Tobin; American Educational Research Association; ERIC record EJ371356
notes: ERIC abstract retrieved through the ERIC API, with the published abstract's threshold statement and the volume, issue and page range confirmed against two further bibliographic records. Used for the definition of wait time as the duration of pauses separating utterances in a verbal exchange, and for the finding that above a threshold of about three seconds teacher and student discourse changed and higher cognitive level achievement was obtained in elementary, middle and high school science, with achievement increases also reported in middle school mathematics. Abstract-level verification; no wording reproduced.

title: Differentiating Instruction in Response to Student Readiness, Interest, and Learning Profile in Academically Diverse Classrooms: A Review of Literature (Journal for the Education of the Gifted, 27(2/3), 119-145)
provider: Carol Ann Tomlinson, Catherine Brighton, Holly Hertberg, Carolyn M. Callahan, Tonya R. Moon, Kay Brimijoin, Lynda A. Conover, Timothy Reynolds; Education Resources Information Center (ERIC EJ787917), IES, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Full text read from the ERIC-hosted PDF. Used for the framing of differentiation as a pedagogical rather than an organizational change; the definition of differentiation as proactive modification of curricula, teaching methods, resources, learning activities and student products; readiness grounded in the zone of proximal development and moderate challenge; the definition of learning profile as a preferred mode of learning shaped by learning style, intelligence preference, gender and culture, together with the authors' own caution that no approach to learning is superior to another; the six hallmarks (proactive, flexible small groups, varied materials, variable pacing, knowledge centered, learner centered); the report of Lou et al. (1996) on within-class grouping; and the closing 'issues requiring further study' section admitting how much was unknown.

title: Review of studies applying Bronfenbrenner's bioecological theory in international and intercultural education research
provider: Peiru Tong and I-Shin An, Frontiers in Psychology 14:1233925 (2024)
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Peer-reviewed open-access review (licence confirmed on the article page). Supports: the 1979 monograph named microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem and macrosystem; the chronosystem came from Bronfenbrenner's later work rather than the original monograph; he subsequently reworked the framework into the Process-Person-Context-Time (bioecological) model; and reviews find that applications which stop at the nested contextual circles and neglect proximal processes misrepresent the theory. Facts synthesised; no prose adapted.

title: Best Alternatives to Cronbach's Alpha Reliability in Realistic Conditions: Congeneric and Asymmetrical Measurements (Frontiers in Psychology, 7:769)
provider: Italo Trizano-Hermosilla and Jesus M. Alvarado; Frontiers Media
license: Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)
